papers.title: Supramolecular Barrel-Stave Anion Channel With Hydroxyl-Rich Selectivity Filter.
papers.abstract: In naturally occurring CLC channels, the hydroxyl groups of serine (Sercen) and tyrosine (Tyrcen) that orient toward the central region of the pore are important for Cl- selectivity. Herein, artificial anion channels with a hydroxyl-rich selectivity filter are reported based on the self-assembly of (R)-(-)-mandelic acid-based derivatives. It was envisaged that multiple monomers would self-assemble in a transmembrane orientation, stabilised by intermolecular hydrogen bonds between the hydroxyl and amide groups of the scaffold, thereby forming the half-channel. Further, the antiparallel, tail-to-tail assembly of two such units would form the channel. Among the derivatives tested, the octyl chain-containing compound 1c exhibited the highest transmembrane transport activity and chloride selectivity. This transport relies on channel-mediated antiport, featuring an average channel diameter of 3.9 ± 0.1 Å and a single-channel conductance of 16.0 ± 0.8 pS. The 1H NMR titration experiment confirmed the major involvement of hydroxyl protons (OH) in chloride binding. Geometry optimisation shows that 1c (17.553 Å) can span half the egg yolk phosphatidylcholine lipid bilayer. Further geometry optimisation confirmed that the pentameric assembly is best suited to form the hydroxyl-rich hydrogen-bonded selectivity filter and to recognise Cl- within the cavity.

papers.title: Heart Rate Surge Improves Cardiovascular Risk Stratification Beyond Hypoxic Burden in Sleep Apnea.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) imposes cardiovascular stress through intermittent hypoxia and event-related responses. Whether heart rate surge adds prognostic information beyond hypoxic burden (HB) remains unclear. The authors aimed to evaluate heart rate surge for cardiovascular mortality and its incremental value beyond HB in OSA. We analyzed 4,790 participants from a community-based cohort with overnight polysomnography. Heart rate surge was defined as peak heart rate within the event-aligned window minus mean heart rate during the 60-second pre-event baseline. Associations with cardiovascular mortality were assessed using Cox models. Incremental prognostic value was evaluated by C-index, net reclassification improvement (NRI), and integrated discrimination improvement. During a median follow-up of 11.6 years (IQR: 10.4-12.4), 334/4,790 participants (7.0%) died of cardiovascular causes. Heart rate surge was weakly correlated with HB (Spearman ρ = 0.08; 95% CI: 0.04-0.10). The highest vs lowest heart rate surge quintile was associated with higher cardiovascular mortality risk (HR: 3.00; 95% CI: 2.10-4.30; P < 0.001) and each 1-SD increment was associated with a 27% higher risk (HR: 1.27; 95% CI: 1.19-1.35). Participants with elevated HB and heart rate surge had the highest risk (HR: 2.65; 95% CI: 1.79-3.92). Adding heart rate surge increased the C-index from 0.77 (95% CI: 0.74-0.79) to 0.81 (95% CI: 0.79-0.83), with ΔC of 0.04 (95% CI: 0.03-0.06), continuous NRI of 0.62 (95% CI: 0.51-0.74), categorical NRI of 0.16 (95% CI: 0.09-0.24), and integrated discrimination improvement of 0.05 (95% CI: 0.04-0.06). Heart rate surge was independently associated with cardiovascular mortality and improved risk stratification beyond HB in OSA.

papers.title: A crosstalk between the immune system and obstructive sleep apnea.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is characterized by recurrent upper airway obstruction during sleep. Its hallmark pathophysiological features, intermittent hypoxia (IH) and sleep fragmentation (SF), trigger cellular and molecular responses that disrupt immune homeostasis. Recurrent hypoxia-reoxygenation promotes oxidative stress and activates hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α), nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB), and the NLRP3 inflammasome, contributing to sustained inflammatory signaling, endothelial dysfunction, and alterations in circulating and tissue-resident immune cells. This review integrates evidence from clinical and preclinical studies linking OSA to dysregulation of innate, adaptive, and humoral immunity and examines how these immune alterations contribute to OSA-associated systemic morbidity. Innate immune dysregulation in OSA is characterized by activation of neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages, increased oxidative stress, and elevated pro-inflammatory mediators, including IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α, CRP, and MCP-1. Altered expressions of ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 may further promote leukocyte recruitment and endothelial dysfunction, sustaining systemic inflammation and end-organ injury. Adaptive immune dysregulation includes alterations in CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell populations, Th1/Th17 polarization, disruption of the Th17/Treg balance, and impaired regulatory T-cell function. Emerging, although comparatively limited, evidence also implicates humoral immune dysregulation. Collectively, the interactions among IH, SF, oxidative stress, inflammation, and immune dysfunction support the concept that OSA is a systemic immune-modulating disorder rather than solely an upper airway disorder. Dysregulation of innate, adaptive, and humoral immunity may contribute to OSA-associated metabolic, cardiovascular, and neurocognitive complications. Defining these immune mechanisms may help explain OSA phenotypic heterogeneity and identify biomarkers of disease severity and therapeutic response. Furthermore, characterization of OSA-specific immune signatures may facilitate patient stratification and advance precision-medicine approaches based on individual inflammatory and immunological phenotypes.

papers.title: Deep brain stimulation as neuroimmune-metabolic modulation in Parkinson's disease and beyond: tissue response, glial remodeling, and disease modification.
papers.abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is an established symptomatic therapy for Parkinson's disease (PD), yet its biological effects extend beyond modulation of abnormal basal ganglia circuitry. This review conceptualizes DBS in PD as a neuroimmune-metabolic intervention acting across the electrode-tissue interface, glial networks, peripheral immunity, and activity-dependent metabolic systems. PD is characterized by convergent immune and metabolic vulnerability. These processes create a disease environment in which electrical stimulation may interact with inflammation, excitotoxicity, bioenergetic stress, and neuronal resilience. We distinguish implantation-related tissue responses from stimulation-induced biological remodeling. Electrode insertion produces acute injury, blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, peri-electrode edema, gliosis, and foreign-body responses, which should not be conflated with the effects of chronic stimulation. Active DBS may modulate central cytokine expression, microglial and astrocytic phenotypes, inflammasome activity, astrocytic glutamate transport, and brain-peripheral immune crosstalk. Emerging evidence also suggests a neurometabolic dimension, including changes in regional glucose utilization, PD-related metabolic network expression, oxidative stress, and neurotrophic signaling. However, these effects are context-dependent and influenced by multiple factors. Although preclinical studies support potential neuroprotective mechanisms involving BDNF/TrkB signaling, mitophagy, reduced excitotoxic-inflammatory coupling, and immune-metabolic rebalancing, clinical evidence remains insufficient to establish DBS as a disease-modifying therapy. Future studies should integrate multiple methods such as longitudinal imaging, electrophysiology, immune profiling and metabolomics. DBS should be understood as a symptomatic circuit-based therapy that may also interact with neuroimmune and metabolic processes, while current evidence remains insufficient to establish a disease-modifying role in PD.

papers.title: Deep brain stimulation and spinal cord stimulation for chronic disorders of consciousness: a decade of clinical evidence, mechanistic insights, and critical appraisal.
papers.abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) and spinal cord stimulation (SCS) have been investigated for over four decades as neuromodulatory treatments for chronic disorders of consciousness (DOC), including the vegetative state/unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (VS/UWS) and the minimally conscious state (MCS), for which no disease-modifying pharmacological therapy exists. This narrative review synthesizes literature published between 2016 and 2026 on the neurobiological rationale, clinical evidence, neurophysiological biomarkers, and safety of DBS and SCS for chronic DOC. The 'mesocircuit hypothesis', supported by human intraoperative electrophysiology and nonhuman primate causal manipulation, provides a coherent rationale for central thalamic and centromedian-parafascicular targeting. Across case series, cohort studies, and individual patient data meta-analyses, both DBS and SCS produce clinically meaningful improvement in a minority of patients, consistently more often in MCS (63-74% response) than in VS/UWS (26-30% response), with younger age and shorter injury-to-treatment interval predicting better outcomes. However, the two largest individual patient data meta-analyses of DBS concur that current evidence is insufficient to conclude that stimulation alters the natural history of neurological recovery beyond what would be expected from patient selection and spontaneous recovery, and adverse event rates (8.1% for SCS, 18.2% for DBS) indicate non-trivial surgical risk in this vulnerable population. Neurophysiological and neuroimaging biomarkers derived from EEG, functional near-infrared spectroscopy, functional MRI, and FDG-PET show promise for objective outcome prediction but await prospective validation. We conclude that DBS and SCS remain experimental, mechanistically motivated but not yet definitively proven therapies for chronic DOC, and that adequately powered randomized controlled trials, biomarker-guided patient selection, and dedicated ethical frameworks are needed before either modality can be recommended outside of research settings.

papers.title: A proposed psychometabolic endotype of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome: bidirectional interplay between psychological distress, eating dysfunction, sleep disruption, chronic stress, and metabolic deterioration.
papers.abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome was renamed polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) in 2026 to better represent its multisystem biology. Psychological distress, eating dysregulation, sleep disturbance, and metabolic dysfunction frequently coexist, yet clinical care and research commonly treat them as parallel comorbidities. To define the proposed psychometabolic construct operationally; position it relative to conventional phenotypes and data-driven clusters; and grade evidence for association, temporal prediction, causation, and treatment response across psychological, behavioral, sleep-stress, neuroendocrine, and metabolic pathways. We conducted a targeted narrative review of PubMed/MEDLINE from inception through 15 September 2026. Seven structured topic blocks returned 1,278 records, 1,009 unique identifiers after PubMed identifier (PMID)-based deduplication, and 1,008 retrievable article records for title/abstract screening. Guidelines, systematic reviews, longitudinal or causal studies, trials, and informative human mechanistic studies were prioritized; general-population and preclinical evidence was used only when its indirectness was explicit. Depression and anxiety, body-image concerns, binge- and bulimia-spectrum symptoms, poor sleep, and obstructive sleep apnea are reported more often in PMOS than in comparison populations, but most estimates are cross-sectional and heterogeneous. One tertiary cohort found that baseline depression and/or anxiety history predicted incident metabolic syndrome over a median seven years (adjusted hazard ratio 1.45, 95% confidence interval 1.02-2.06); this supports prognostic enrichment, not causality. General-population longitudinal and genetic studies support reciprocal depression-metabolic relationships, whereas PMOS-specific causal evidence is inconsistent. Plausible links include insulin-androgen-adipose interactions, neuroactive steroid signaling, ovarian sympathetic input, sleep fragmentation, stress and autonomic regulation, reward-related eating, treatment exposure, stigma, and social context. None validates a discrete endotype. We define a candidate psychometabolic endotype as a cross-cutting, mechanistically coupled pattern that may occur within any conventional PMOS phenotype. Clinical co-occurrence is only an entry profile; endotype status requires replicated longitudinal coupling, incremental prognostic value, interpretable transitions, and preferably treatment-effect heterogeneity. Four overlapping prototypes are working formulations rather than subtypes. A six-step clinical pathway centers shared formulation and nests care-intensity tiers within treatment selection.

papers.title: Glycosides of Cistanche improve cognitive dysfunction in sleep-deprived model rats by activating the SIRT1/PGC-1α/Nrf2 signaling pathway.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation suppresses the SIRT1/PGC-1α/Nrf2 signaling pathway, leading to oxidative stress, synaptic damage, and cognitive dysfunction. Glycosides of Cistanche (GCs) possess well-documented antioxidant and neuroprotective properties and have been reported to improve cognition in sleep-deprived animals, but the molecular mechanism remains unclear. We hypothesized that GCs alleviate sleep deprivation-induced cognitive dysfunction by activating the SIRT1/PGC-1α/Nrf2 signaling pathway. Sixty male Sprague Dawley rats were randomly assigned to six groups (n = 10): Control, Platform, Model, GCs, Control+GCs, and Estazolam (Est) groups. A 21-day sleep deprivation model was established using the modified multiple platform water method. Assessments included cognitive function by Morris water maze (MWM) test; Wake, non-rapid eye movement (NREM), rapid eye movement (REM), and total sleep time (TST) by Electroencephalogram (EEG); the serum levels of MDA, GSH-Px and SOD by ELISA, hippocampal CA1 neuronal morphology structure by Nissl staining and transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and the SIRT1/PGC-1α/Nrf2 signaling pathway and synaptic related proteins were detected by Western blot. In an additional cohort (n = 40), the SIRT1-specific inhibitor EX527 was used to validate the causal role of the pathway. Compared with the Control group, the Model group exhibited significantly prolonged escape latency, along with reduced the number of platform crossings and the percentage time in the target quadrant (p < 0.05). The proportion of Wake significantly increased, while NREM, REM, and TST all significantly decreased (all p < 0.01). The serum level of MDA elevated, while GSH-Px and SOD activities markedly reduced (all p < 0.01). Hippocampal CA1 neurons showed disorganized arrangement, decreased Nissl bodies, and mitochondrial damage. Moreover, the SIRT1/PGC-1α/Nrf2 signaling pathway and synaptic related proteins significantly downregulated (all p < 0.01). Nevertheless, GCs intervention ameliorated cognitive dysfunction, alleviated oxidative stress and neuronal damage, and upregulated the protein expression levels above mentioned (all p < 0.01). Notably, these protective effects of GCs were abrogated by the SIRT1 inhibitor EX527. GCs inhibited oxidative stress damage and improved synaptic plasticity, and thereby alleviated sleep deprivation induced cognitive dysfunction by activating the SIRT1/PGC-1α/Nrf2 signaling pathway.

papers.title: Reasons for encounter and recommended interventions in an interprofessional integrative oncology counseling program in outpatient care: a mixed-methods analysis of 1,693 consultation letters.
papers.abstract: Complementary and integrative healthcare (CIH) approaches play an increasingly important role in oncology care, involving a wide range of healthcare professionals and therapeutic methods. While patient demand for CIH and the evidence base for individual interventions have grown considerably, the implementation of structured counseling services for the effective and safe use of CIH remains limited. To address this gap, a controlled, multicenter implementation study was conducted at four Comprehensive Cancer Centers (CCC) in Germany to establish an outpatient, interprofessional, evidence-based counseling service for CIH (CCC-Integrativ). This mixed-methods study investigates the specific reasons for encounter (RfE) and the recommended interventions during these consultations. Patients enrolled in the CCC-Integrativ study received three CIH consultations within a three-month period, the first of which was conducted jointly by specifically trained physicians and nurses. After each session, a consultation letter was prepared summarizing the main patient RfE and recommendations. All consultation letters were analyzed using qualitative content analysis, and the results were subsequently analyzed quantitatively. A total of 1,693 consultation letters from 603 oncology patients were analyzed. The most frequent reasons for encounter included general weakness and fatigue (56%), chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (40%), sleep disturbances (37%), and general pain (36%). Nearly all patients received counseling on lifestyle modifications, including nutrition (95%), physical activity (93%), and stress management (81%). Additionally, an average of 15 specific CIH interventions were recommended per patient, encompassing naturopathic nursing interventions (97%), herbal medicines and teas (79%), acupressure (79%), and mindfulness-based movement therapies (44%). Interprofessional outpatient counseling on CIH in oncology addresses a wide spectrum of patient RfE, provides guidance on lifestyle modifications, and offers specific, individualized CIH interventions to help patients manage burdensome symptoms. These findings suggest that interprofessional integrative counseling services can play a crucial role in outpatient oncology care by providing a holistic approach tailored to individual needs. Furthermore, structured integrative oncology counseling may serve a valuable navigational role within outpatient care settings.

papers.title: Sleep, executive functions, and repetitive behaviors in autism spectrum disorder: different patterns of association with lower- and higher-level repetitive behaviors.
papers.abstract: Restricted and repetitive behaviors (RBs) are a core feature of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), although the mechanisms underlying different RB subtypes remain poorly understood. The present study investigated the differential contribution of executive functions (EFs) to lower- and higher-level RBs in autistic children and explored whether specific EF domains mediated the relationship between sleep disturbances and RBs. Fifty-seven autistic children aged 6-14 years underwent neuropsychological and behavioral assessment. RBs were assessed using the Repetitive Behavior Scale-Revised, executive functions using the Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function-2, sleep disturbances through the Sleep Disturbance Scale for Children, and behavioral difficulties through the Child Behavior Checklist. Partial correlations, regression analyses, and mediation models were performed. Distinct association patterns emerged across RB subtypes. Lower-level RBs were significantly associated only with emotional control difficulties, whereas higher-level RBs were associated with several EF domains, including inhibition, shifting, emotional control, planning, and initiation. Regression analyses showed that higher-level RBs were independently predicted by shifting difficulties, whereas lower-level RBs were significantly associated with IQ and behavioral problems. Mediation analyses indicated that emotional control difficulties significantly explained the association between sleep disturbances and lower-level RBs. In contrast, cognitive flexibility did not mediate the relationship between sleep disturbances and higher-level RBs. These findings provide preliminary evidence of different patterns of association across lower- and higher-level RBs in autistic children. Emotional regulation processes may be particularly relevant for lower-level RBs, whereas cognitive flexibility appears more strongly related to higher-level RBs. Findings also suggest that sleep disturbances may contribute to specific RB manifestations through different mechanisms.

papers.title: Clinical and resting-state EEG changes following neurofeedback in adult refugees with persistent trauma-related symptoms: a transdiagnostic pre-post observational study.
papers.abstract: Neurofeedback has shown promise as an adjunctive intervention for persistent trauma-related psychopathology, but its electrophysiological effects in refugees following war, torture, and forced displacement remain poorly understood. This study investigated changes in resting-state alpha electrophysiology during trauma treatment incorporating individualised neurofeedback and whether these changes related to clinical improvement. This retrospective pre-post observational study included 53 adult refugees with persistent trauma-related symptoms who completed resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) before and after multidisciplinary treatment incorporating neurofeedback, trauma-focused counselling and pharmacotherapy. Participants received a mean of 38.7 neurofeedback sessions after remaining symptomatic despite previous treatment. Clinical improvement was assessed retrospectively using the Clinical Global Impression-Improvement (CGI-I) scale. Resting-state EEG analyses examined changes in global alpha amplitude, alpha reactivity, peak alpha frequency (PAF), and alpha coherence. Neurofeedback protocol implementation was characterised across 2,361 protocol applications, and secondary analyses examined electrophysiological differences between responders and non-responders and associations between electrophysiological and clinical change. Thirty-three participants (62.3%) demonstrated clinically meaningful improvement following multidisciplinary treatment incorporating neurofeedback. Resting-state EEG demonstrated increased global alpha amplitude (FDR-adjusted p = .018) and reduced occipital alpha reactivity (FDR-adjusted p = .013), whereas peak alpha frequency and alpha coherence did not change significantly following correction for multiple comparisons. Exploratory analyses suggested different patterns of eyes-open and eyes-closed alpha change in responders and non-responders; however, the difference between groups was not statistically significant (t(51) = 0.88, p = .381, d = 0.24). Changes in electrophysiological measures were not significantly associated with clinical improvement. Protocol analysis demonstrated variability in electrode placement, whereas reward frequencies remained clustered within the alpha range throughout treatment. Individualised neurofeedback delivered within routine multidisciplinary care was associated with clinically meaningful improvement in two-thirds of refugees with persistent trauma-related psychopathology, alongside selective changes in resting-state alpha electrophysiology. These findings extend current understanding of the electrophysiological changes observed during treatment incorporating neurofeedback in a clinically complex refugee population. Although the retrospective observational design limits conclusions regarding causality, the findings support investigation of neurofeedback as an adjunctive intervention for refugees who remain symptomatic despite previous treatment and identify resting-state alpha reactivity as a promising electrophysiological measure of treatment-associated change.

papers.title: Neural oscillatory activity during guided and self-generated motor imagery: a comparative case study of a six-time World Cup skateboarder champion and an experienced recreational surfer.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to examine and compare neural oscillatory activity during guided and self-generated motor imagery in two individuals with contrasting levels of competitive expertise: a six-time World Cup skateboarder champion and an experienced recreational surfer. Following baseline recording, continuous electroencephalographic (EEG) activity (Brain Products GmbH, Gilching, Germany) was acquired during three motor imagery conditions: verbally guided training imagery, verbally guided competition imagery, and self-generated competition imagery. Analyses of frontal alpha asymmetry (FAA), frontal beta asymmetry (FBA), and frontal midline theta (fmθ) showed distinct patterns of frontal oscillatory activity across imagery conditions and between the two athletes. FAA and FBA values were consistently lower in the skateboarder than in the surfer during the imagery conditions, although between-case differences were already evident at baseline. In contrast, fmθ showed a condition-dependent pattern, with higher values in the skateboarder during verbally guided training imagery but lower values during verbally guided and self-generated competition imagery. These case-level observations suggest that frontal oscillatory activity during motor imagery may vary according to imagery condition and individual characteristics. However, because the two participants differed not only in competitive expertise but also in sport discipline, prior imagery training, and trait imagery ability, the observed EEG differences cannot be attributed specifically to motor expertise. Accordingly, these findings should be considered preliminary and hypothesis-generating, providing a basis for future studies examining the relationships among motor expertise, imagery modality, and neural oscillatory activity in larger and more homogeneous samples.

papers.title: Sex differences in sleep architecture among patients with severe mental disorders: a polysomnographic study.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are common in severe mental illness, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and major depressive disorder. Yet sex-specific sleep patterns across schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and major depressive disorder remain poorly characterized. In this cross-sectional study, we compared overnight polysomnography between 372 first-episode patients (aged 18-45) (93 schizophrenia, 181 major depressive disorder, 98 bipolar disorder). All participants underwent a single-night 10-channel polysomnography. After controlling for age, illness duration, BMI, and medications, women achieved significantly longer total sleep time (median 449.3 vs 420.3 min; p <0.001), time in bed (543.0 vs 525.5 min; p = 0.03), and higher sleep efficiency (83.3% vs 82.3%; p = 0.004) than men. Exploratory post-hoc analyses revealed potential sex-related differences in major depressive disorder and bipolar disorder (all p < 0.05, uncorrected for multiple comparisons). However, these findings did not survive correction for multiple comparisons, indicating that the observed differences should be interpreted with caution as preliminary. This study found that biological sex modulated sleep macro-architecture in severe mental illness, with women exhibiting longer sleep duration and higher sleep efficiency relative to men. Although the cross-diagnosis comparison revealed only a marginally significant sex-by-diagnosis interaction that did not persist after multiple testing correction, these exploratory subgroup findings suggest potential nuanced variations in sleep architecture. Consequently, future studies with larger cohorts are warranted to evaluate whether sex-stratified approaches could refine clinical sleep interventions across psychiatric conditions.

papers.title: A brain functional network framework based on EEG connectivity for major depressive disorder recognition.
papers.abstract: When the brain is regarded as a complex dynamic system, its abnormalities often show the overall network reorganization. Traditional analysis for major depressive disorder (MDD) based on single-channel features of electroencephalogram (EEG) mainly focuses on signal changes, while ignoring inter-regional functional connectivity and network topology. As a consequence, it is challenging to reveal the systemic abnormal mechanisms. To address this problem, this study built a framework of multi-frequency brain functional network (BFN) construction and recognition based on resting-state EEG. Phase-locking value (PLV) and Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) were separately utilized to characterize phase synchronization and amplitude correlation. Abnormal BFNs in MDD were systematically evaluated from both connectivity patterns and node topology. Results suggest that MDD patients exhibit increased connectivity in the left frontal, central, and parietal regions in the low-frequency bands. In the mid-frequency bands, increased fronto-central connectivity and reduced posterior connectivity are observed. In the high-frequency band, the connectivity pattern is characterized by increased fronto-temporal and centro-temporal connectivity, together with reduced connectivity in the posterior regions. At the node level, the most prominent alterations are concentrated in the parietal region, particularly in the α band, where altered betweenness centrality (BC) is consistently identified across both PLV and PCC networks. On this basis, the support vector machine (SVM) classifier was employed to evaluate the discriminative capability of PLV-Edge, PCC-Edge, PLV-Node, and PCC-Node features for MDD identification. Among the four feature types, PLV-Node features achieve the highest mean classification balanced accuracy of 81.44%, and PCC-Node features achieve a mean balanced accuracy of 79.14%. All four feature types demonstrate discriminative potential for distinguishing patients with MDD from healthy controls (HCs). These findings suggest that functional connectivity-based brain network features may provide meaningful information for the auxiliary identification of MDD.

papers.title: Graded multisensory neurofeedback via the iNems system for comprehensive upper limb recovery after stroke: a multiple baseline study.
papers.abstract: Post-stroke upper-limb recovery remains challenging, especially in the presence of sensory impairments. Conventional brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) are constrained by binary feedback, single-modality stimulation, and exclusion of patients with sensory deficits. We developed the Imagery Neurofeedback-based Multi-sensory System (iNems), a neurofeedback system that provides graded multisensory (visual and electrical) feedback based on ERD magnitude. This study validated iNems' efficacy in motor function, self-reported numbness, and cognitive functions using a multiple-baseline design (MBD). Four participants with post-stroke upper-limb motor and sensory impairments underwent a multiple baseline design. The baseline phase (phase A) used random feedback; the intervention (phase B) used adaptive iNems. iNems quantified motor intention via sensorimotor EEG event-related desynchronization (ERD) and delivered graded visual and electrical feedback. Primary outcomes were the Fugl-Meyer Assessment-Upper Extremity (FMA-UE) and Box and Block Test (BBT). Secondary outcomes included body cognition, numbness, and neurophysiological (ERD/ERS) changes. All participants demonstrated significant improvement during the intervention. FMA-UE increased by 6-16 points. The BBT showed large effects (integrated Tau-U = 0.75). Body cognition improved significantly in both sense of agency (Tau-U = 0.80) and ownership (Tau-U = 0.89). Numbness was reduced in affected cases (Tau-U = -0.85). Neurophysiological changes correlated with functional gains, with some patterns suggesting increased neural efficiency. This first MBD-validated demonstration shows that graded, multisensory graded neurofeedback based on ERD magnitude can improve motor, self-reported numbness, and cognitive domains after stroke. These findings support adaptive closed-loop therapy as a promising, multifaceted rehabilitation strategy.

papers.title: Reward positivity and affective functioning in early childhood: evidence from temporospatial principal components analysis.
papers.abstract: Reward-related Positivity (RewP) indexes neural sensitivity to reward feedback and has been widely studied in adolescents and adults. However, little is known about how individual differences in RewP are associated with emotional functioning during early childhood, a critical period for affective development. Interpretation of feedback-related ERPs in children is further complicated by temporally overlapping components. This study examined whether a principal component analysis (PCA)-derived RewP is associated with affective functioning in children aged 4-7 years. Electroencephalography was recorded from 140 children during an age-appropriate reward task. Temporospatial PCA was performed on the full EEG sample (n = 140), and primary regression analyses were conducted in the subset with complete covariate data (n = 48). Temporospatial PCA was applied to isolate a RewP component differentiating gain from loss feedback. Positive and negative affect were assessed using the child version of the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule. Regression analyses examined whether PCA-derived RewP- and gain-related P200 amplitudes were associated with affective functioning while controlling for age, sex, ethnicity, income-to-need ratio, child depressive symptoms, and parental depressive symptoms. At the group level, boys showed greater PCA-derived gain-related P200 amplitudes than girls. At the individual level, higher child positive affect was associated with larger PCA-derived RewP amplitudes in the primary covariate-adjusted regression model. In sensitivity analyses conducted in the larger sample without the income-to-needs covariate, negative affect, rather than positive affect, was significantly associated with PCA-derived RewP amplitude. These findings provide novel evidence that RewP may serve as an early neural marker of affective functioning. By extending RewP research to an understudied developmental period and emphasizing normative emotional functioning, this study advances understanding of early reward processing and highlights the utility of PCA for isolating meaningful ERP components in children.

papers.title: Trajectories of postoperative fatigue and their association with physical and mental health among patients with peritoneal metastases from colorectal and appendiceal cancer after cytoreductive surgery and hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy: a 1-year longitudinal study.
papers.abstract: Postoperative fatigue (POF) is a common complication following major or medium-sized surgeries. It is influenced by surgical trauma, pain, sleep quality, nutrition, and mental state, and can significantly hinder postoperative recovery. As enhanced recovery protocols become more widely adopted in perioperative care, attention to the prevention and management of POF has increased. This 1-year longitudinal study enrolled patients with peritoneal metastases from colorectal and appendiceal cancer following cytoreductive surgery and hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (CRS-HIPEC) at two tertiary hospitals. Participants completed self-administered questionnaires at discharge, and at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months after surgery. POF was assessed using the 10-item Identity-Consequence Fatigue Scale (ICFS-10). Group-based trajectory modeling (GBTM) was utilized to identify distinct POF trajectories, and multivariable models were fitted to examine their associations with sleep quality, pain, and physical and mental conditions over time. The reporting of this study adhered to the Guidelines for Reporting on Latent Trajectory Studies (GRoLTS) checklist. Among 182 participants who experienced POF during follow-up, three distinct fatigue trajectories were identified: high-increasing (29.67%), moderate-increasing (37.36%), and low-increasing (31.87%). Poor sleep quality, inadequate pain management, and compromised physical and mental conditions were linked to trajectory groups with more severe fatigue symptoms. After adjusting for covariates, the high-increasing trajectory group demonstrated significantly lower scores in mental dimensions at 12 months post-discharge. This study presents the cumulative incidence and longitudinal trajectories of POF over a 1-year postoperative period, analyzing the relationship between physical and mental conditions in peritoneal metastatic cancer survivors. Our findings underscore the importance of early identification and targeted treatment of high-risk patients to prevent the chronic progression of POF. These trajectory patterns provide potential clinical avenues for the early detection and management of persistent fatigue based on a patient's evolving symptom profile.

papers.title: Sleep disturbances promote colorectal cancer perineural invasion via GABA-mediated BDNF secretion.
papers.abstract: Perineural invasion (PNI) is a hallmark of aggressive colorectal cancer (CRC) progression, often leading to poor patient outcomes. Emerging evidence suggests a link between sleep disturbances and cancer progression through neural pathways. In this study, we investigated how sleep disturbances contribute to PNI in CRC via γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). Clinical data revealed that CRC patients with poor sleep quality exhibited higher PNI rates and worse prognoses. Sleep-deprived mice showed increased CNS-derived GABA levels and compromised blood-brain barrier integrity, facilitating peripheral GABA exposure. GABA treatment enhanced CRC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion by upregulating FOS expression, which in turn increased BDNF secretion. Elevated BDNF activated Schwann cells through the TrkB receptor, promoting their proliferation, migration, invasion, and angiogenesis. Knockdown of FOS or inhibition of TrkB mitigated these effects. Additionally, GABA was found to promote FOS transcription via upregulation of EGR1. Our findings unveil a novel mechanism whereby sleep disturbances exacerbate CRC progression through the GABA-EGR1-FOS-BDNF axis, highlighting the importance of sleep quality in CRC management and suggesting potential therapeutic targets to inhibit PNI.

papers.title: Disability and its correlates among older adults with common mental disorders in China: a 5-year follow-up study.
papers.abstract: Common mental disorders (CMDs) represent a category of conditions characterized by a high rate of disability and a significant social burden. This study aims to describe disability at baseline and five years later among older adults with 12-month CMDs and to investigate its correlates. Based on the nationally representative China Mental Health Survey (CMHS), a five-year follow-up cohort study was conducted, in which older adults with 12-month common mental disorders (CMDs) at baseline were reassessed. Follow-up assessments were conducted by telephone, and disability was measured using the World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0. Disability prevalence at baseline and five-year follow-up and its correlates were analysed. The baseline analyses included 582 older adults with CMDs, of whom 134 completed the five-year follow-up and were included in the follow-up analyses. The prevalence of disability at baseline and five years later were 57.1% and 19.3%, respectively. Older age (≥70 years vs. 60-64 years: RR = 1.12, 95% CI: 1.06-1.19), residence in the Western region (vs. Eastern: RR = 1.09, 95% CI: 1.02-1.16), physical comorbidity (1-2 diseases: RR = 1.10, 95% CI: 1.02-1.18; ≥3 diseases: RR = 1.31, 95% CI: 1.22-1.41), comorbidity of multiple CMDs (RR = 1.21, 95% CI: 1.14-1.29), and sleep disturbances (RR = 1.17, 95% CI: 1.10-1.24) were associated with higher disability scores. Higher educational level (junior high school and above vs. literate or below primary school) was associated with lower long-term disability among participants with CMDs (RR = 0.85; 95% CI: 0.74-0.97). Living in urban areas (RR = 0.80; 95% CI: 0.69-0.92) was associated with lower long-term disability among individuals with anxiety disorders. Long-term disability persists among older adults with CMDs who survived and were reachable despite an overall decline. Modifiable factors, including physical and mental comorbidity and sleep disturbances, were associated with higher baseline disability, whereas higher education and urban living were associated with a reduced risk of long-term disability. Integrated interventions are needed to reduce disability burden.

papers.title: Postpartum needs and experiences of young and first-time mothers in northwestern Tanzania.
papers.abstract: To explore postpartum needs and lived experiences of young and first-time mothers in northwestern Tanzania. This descriptive, phenomenological, qualitative study was conducted between April and July 2022. Participants included young mothers (<20 years old) and first-time mothers within 6 weeks postpartum. Data were collected via 20 in-depth interviews (IDIs) and seven focus group discussions (FGDs) with 42 participants from government health facilities in Mwanza City. The interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed, translated into English, and analyzed using inductive thematic analysis. The majority of participants (77.8%) were first-time mothers; 69.4% of the respondents were aged 25-35 years. Three themes emerged: postpartum needs, positive experiences, and negative experiences. Postpartum needs included informational support, psychological support, and practical assistance. Positive experiences included pride in motherhood, bonding with the infant, and increased confidence. Negative experiences included sleep disturbances, breastfeeding challenges, changes in appetite, anxiety, and emotional distress, exacerbated by limited support. Young and first-time mothers face significant physical, emotional, and informational challenges in the postpartum period. Strengthening social support and targeted postnatal interventions is critical to improving maternal and infant outcomes in high-burden settings.

papers.title: Behavioral and psychosocial correlates of fasting blood glucose in a resource-constrained diabetes clinic in the Dominican Republic: an exploratory network analysis.
papers.abstract: Examine the associations between demographic, behavioral, and psychosocial characteristics and fasting blood glucose among adults with type 2 diabetes (T2D) at a regional diabetes clinic in the Dominican Republic (DR). This cross-sectional study enrolled 65 adults with T2D who received care from a non-profit regional diabetes clinic in the DR. Participants completed interviewer-administered questionnaires to assess sleep quality, perceived stress, diet quality, health-related quality-of-life, and physical activity (PA). Fasting blood glucose was measured using capillary testing by a clinic nurse. A complete-case network analysis was conducted to examine conditional associations among study variables. Only 15 participants (23%) had fasting blood glucose within the 80-130 mg•dL-1 target range for people with T2D, with significantly higher levels among men (243 ± 93 vs. 170 ± 64 mg•dL-1, p<0.001). Participants reported poor sleep quality (98%), moderate-to-high stress (97%), and low consumption of fruits and vegetables. Although 95% of participants met or exceeded recommended PA volume, activity was primarily from occupational and household tasks performed at light-to-moderate intensity. PA was the most connected variable within the network, and was inversely related to fasting blood glucose. In this resource-constrained DR clinic sample, poor fasting blood glucose coexisted with substantial sleep, stress, and diet deficiencies, despite substantial low-to-moderate-intensity PA. The network findings support diabetes self-management interventions to improve physical activity, sleep hygiene, stress reduction, and diet education, to improve glycemic control in low- and middle-income countries. Future prospective network analyses may identify context-specific behavioral targets for improving glycemic control in similar populations.
papers.journal: Frontiers in clinical diabetes and healthcare

papers.title: A study on the effects of virtual high-altitude exposure on brain function activity in people with different severity of fear of heights.
papers.abstract: The electroencephalography (EEG) microstate method has been extensively used to investigate brain function activity in patients with mental disorders. However, previous studies mainly focused on the analysis of basic microstate features. In this study, we aimed to explore brain electrical activities of individuals with different severity of fear of heights (FoH) during virtual high-altitude exposure using power spectrum and functional brain network based on microstate EEG. First, 69 male participants were included and classified into one of three degrees of FoH (i.e., no-FoH, mild or moderate FoH (m-FoH) and severe FoH (s-FoH)) according to their acrophobia questionnaire (AQ) scores. Then, 32-channel EEG signals were recorded from each subject during virtual high-altitude exposure. Subsequently, microstate EEG signals and corresponding microstate time windows for all subjects were obtained by the microstate analysis. Finally, the Welch method and weighted phase lag index were applied to these signals to compute microstate power spectrum features and brain network properties, and these measures were compared among three groups. The results showed that the s-FoH group had significantly higher relative delta power than the no-FoH group for microstates B and F, and than the m-FoH group for microstates B, C and F. In constrast, the s-FoH group had lower relative alpha power than no-FoH group for microstates B, D and F, and than m-FoH group for microstates D and F. These differences were observed in multiple brain regions, mainly including the frontal and frontal-central areas. The s-FoH group also exhibited a significantly larger power ratio theta/alpha in the frontal-central region for microstates B, C, D and F compared to the no-FoH group, and in the central region for microstate D relative to the m-FoH group. Moreover, these features of microstate power spectrum with significant differences between different FoH groups significantly associated with the scores of AQ. For microstate functional brain network, prominently increased clustering coefficient and local efficiency were observed in both the m-FoH and s-FoH (i.e. FoH) groups for microstate F compared to the no-FoH group. It was also found that FoH individuals have significantly reduced robustness of microstate brain network F. Regarding degree distribution, the FoH groups exhibited power law distributions in microstate brain network A, whereas the no-FoH group displayed exponentially truncated power law patterns, which was opposite for microstate D. In summary, our findings revealed the disrupted power spectrum and functional brain network in individuals with FoH during virtual high-altitude exposure from the perspective of microstate EEG, which may advance our understanding of the neuropathology of fear of heights and provide a novel electrophysiological tool for its clinical assessment. However, to control the influence of gender and age on fear responses and EEG dynamics, only young male participants in their early twenties were recruited. Therefore, the present findings should be interpreted with caution, and their generalizability to female populations and older adults remains to be verified.

papers.title: Association between nocturia frequency and depression in adults: evidence from NHANES 2021-2023 and a Chinese exploratory cohort.
papers.abstract: Nocturia and depression commonly coexist and may share underlying pathways. We examined the cross-sectional association between nocturia frequency and clinically relevant depressive symptoms. We analyzed 4,162 adults from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2021-2023. Nocturia was categorized as 0, 1, 2, or ≥3 voids/night; a Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) score ≥10 defined clinically relevant depressive symptoms. Survey-weighted logistic regression, an ordinal trend test, and subgroup analyses were conducted. A Chinese cohort (n = 255) was used for exploratory sleep-pathway analyses. A sensitivity analysis used a modified Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) score excluding the sleep-disturbance component, which includes the nocturnal bathroom-use item. In the fully adjusted complex survey model, two voids/night (OR: 1.42; 95% CI: 1.05-1.92; p = 0.026) and ≥3 voids/night (OR: 1.83; 95% CI: 1.40-2.40; p < 0.001) were associated with higher odds of clinically relevant depressive symptoms, with an ordinal trend (p < 0.001). An exploratory age interaction was observed (Wald p for interaction = 0.043). In the Chinese exploratory cohort, the unstandardized indirect effect through total PSQI score was 0.244 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.094-0.426), whereas the total and direct effects were non-significant. A sensitivity analysis excluding the PSQI sleep-disturbance component yielded a smaller but still positive indirect effect (0.181; bootstrap 95% CI 0.053-0.342). Frequent nocturia was cross-sectionally associated with clinically relevant depressive symptoms. The Chinese exploratory outpatient cohort provided exploratory support for a sleep-related statistical pathway, which was attenuated but remained positive after excluding the PSQI sleep-disturbance component. These findings highlight nocturia as a clinically relevant symptom linking urinary, sleep, and mental health, while longitudinal studies are needed to clarify temporal and causal relationships.

papers.title: Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated isolated seizures in children: a retrospective single-center case series.
papers.abstract: Isolated seizures represent a distinct, rare, and underrecognized phenotype of myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) antibody-associated disease (MOGAD). In recent years, documentation of this phenotype has been limited to sporadic reports, with dedicated case series being extremely scarce. This study aimed to describe the clinical characteristics of isolated seizures in pediatric patients with MOGAD. We retrospectively reviewed the medical records of pediatric patients diagnosed with MOG antibody-associated isolated seizures between January 2019 and January 2026. Clinical manifestations, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings, laboratory data, treatment regimens, and clinical outcomes were systematically analyzed. Among the cohort of 172 pediatric patients with seropositive MOG antibodies, 6 (3.4%) met the inclusion criteria for isolated seizures. The median age at onset was 7.5 years (range, 5-9 years), with a male-to-female ratio of 1:2. Clinically, 4 patients presented solely with epileptic seizures, while the other 2 patients had additional transient limb weakness or headache, respectively. Focal seizures were observed in 5 patients, including 3 with focal motor seizures; additionally, 2 cases experienced status epilepticus. No patients exhibited encephalopathy or focal neurological deficits. Four patients had peripheral blood leukocytosis (range, 11.9-26 × 109/L), and five had elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rates (ESR; range, 22-43 mm/h). All six patients showed cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pleocytosis (41.1 ± 20.4/μL; range, 15-69/μL) without detectable infectious pathogens. Abnormal electroencephalogram (EEG) findings, including abnormal background activity and focal slow waves, were identified in 3 patients. No cranial MRI abnormalities were detected in any patient. All patients received immunotherapy, with one patient additionally receiving anti-seizure medications (ASMs). At final follow-up, all patients had favorable outcomes, with no recurrence of seizures or subsequent demyelinating events. Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated isolated seizures is a rare and frequently underrecognized phenotype within the spectrum of MOGAD. For school-age children presenting with epileptic seizures, particularly focal motor seizures, along with elevated ESR and CSF pleocytosis, early testing for MOG antibody is recommended in the absence of clinical or radiological evidence of encephalitis or focal neurological deficits. Most patients achieve favorable clinical outcomes, which may be partially attributed to immunotherapy. However, the efficacy of immunotherapy in preventing seizure recurrence, subsequent demyelinating events, and subclinical radiological disease remains indeterminate.

papers.title: Patient-reported propagated sensation along meridians during acupuncture for lumbar disc herniation: protocol for an exploratory prospective cohort study with multimodal neurophysiological and immune measurements.
papers.abstract: Propagated sensation along meridians (PSM) refers to the radiation of needling sensation beyond the needling site along meridian pathways. In traditional acupuncture theory, PSM has long been considered an important factor associated with clinical efficacy, particularly in conditions like lumbar disc herniation where pain radiates along the lower limb. However, this phenomenon has not been well characterized by modern neurobiological methods. Whether patients who report PSM show distinct autonomic, sensory, or motor responses, and whether this relates to better outcomes, remains unclear. In this study, we aim to explore the clinical and physiological correlates of patient-reported PSM in a cohort of LDH patients receiving standardized acupuncture. This single-center, prospective, observational cohort study will enroll 204 LDH patients with radicular pain. Participants will be classified into three groups based on PSM reporting across three treatment sessions corroborated by assessor-documented needle-evoked muscle twitches: PSM-positive, PSM-negative, and indeterminate. The primary endpoint is the clinical improvement rate based on Japanese Orthopaedic Association (JOA) scores. Secondary endpoints include pain intensity (VAS), functional status (JOA), multimodal neurophysiological parameters (EEG, sEMG, EDA, EOG), serological cytokine profiles (IL-1β, IL-2, IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-12p70, IL-17, IFN-γ, TNF-α, and IFN-α), and the Massachusetts General Hospital Acupuncture Sensation Scale (MASS) administered post-session to quantify PSM intensity and spreading. Data will be analyzed using linear mixed-effects models, with results reported as effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals and false discovery rate correction within signal families; exploratory multimodal analyses will be used to identify physiological features associated with PSM. We hypothesize that the PSM-positive cohort will show greater clinical improvement than the PSM-negative cohort, with larger reductions in radicular pain and better functional recovery following standardized acupuncture. papers.title: Conventional and novel hypoxemia-related indices for obstructive sleep apnea severity and incident hypertension: a prospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is associated with hypertension (HTN), but the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) and oxygen desaturation index (ODI) may not fully characterize nocturnal hypoxemia relevant to HTN development. We evaluated the associations of the sleep breathing impairment index (SBII) and hypoxic burden (HB) with incident HTN and compared their discriminative performance with AHI and ODI. This prospective study included 601 participants with OSA (AHI ≥ 15 events/h) from Sleep Heart Health Study who were free of HTN at baseline. SBII, HB, AHI and ODI were analyzed both in quartiles and as continuous variables. Multivariable logistic regression and restricted cubic spline analyses were used to evaluate their associations with incident HTN. Discrimination performance was assessed by comparing a clinical base model with models that separately incorporating each quartile-categorized index. During a median follow-up of approximately 5 years, 194 (32.3%) participants developed HTN. In the primary fully adjusted model, the highest quartiles of SBII (OR, 1.71; 95% CI, 1.02-2.90; p = 0.044) and HB (OR, 1.69; 95% CI, 1.02-2.79; p = 0.041) were associated with higher odds of incident HTN. In the T90-adjusted sensitivity model, both associations were significant, whereas AHI and ODI quartiles remained nonsignificant. The clinical base model had a C-statistic of 0.614; adding SBII or HB, did not significantly improve discrimination. Exploratory quartile-based analyses suggested that the highest quartiles of SBII and HB were associated with higher odds of incident HTN among participants with OSA, whereas AHI and ODI were not. These findings indicate that marked elevation in SBII and HB may provide a more comprehensive characterization of OSA-related nocturnal hypoxemia relevant to incident HTN. However, the nonsignificant continuous and overall spline analyses and the limited incremental discrimination warrant cautious interpretation and further validation.

papers.title: Clinical phenotypes and outcomes of spinal cord stimulation in painful peripheral polyneuropathy: a cohort including diabetic, chemotherapy-induced, and idiopathic etiologies.
papers.abstract: Chronic painful peripheral polyneuropathy (PPN) is a leading global cause of chronic pain and may arise from a wide range of etiologies. When pharmacological treatments fail to provide adequate pain relief, spinal cord stimulation (SCS) has demonstrated efficacy in selected subtypes. This study investigated the effectiveness of SCS in alleviating pain, neurological symptoms and signs, and other health-related outcomes in patients with diverse forms of PPN, including diabetic (DPN) and chemotherapy-induced (CIPN) peripheral neuropathies, and chronic idiopathic axonal polyneuropathy (CIAP). This prospective, single-center observational study included 30 patients with drug-refractory PPN (11 DPN, 8 CIPN, 9 CIAP, and 2 other etiologies: 1 amyloidosis and 1 Fabry disease). All patients were implanted with two percutaneous leads at T10-T11 targeting lower limbs; a cervical lead (C4-C7) when upper limb pain was present; and SCS system. Low-frequency (<100 Hz) sub-perception and/or supra-perception stimulation modalities were offered. Clinical outcomes were assessed at baseline and at 2, 4, 6, and 12 months post-implantation and included pain (VAS, SF-MPQ-2), neuropathic symptoms (NPSI), autonomic symptoms (SAS), neurological signs, and other health-related factors. Intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD) was assessed at baseline and at 12 months. Baseline evaluations demonstrated severe disease burden, with CIAP patients exhibiting more pain symptoms and DPN patients more neurologic deficits. SCS produced a significant and sustained reduction in pain intensity and symptoms (VAS from 8.6 to 2.0, SF-MPQ-2 from 115.5 to 23.0; p < 0.001) across all PPN subtypes, with greater improvements observed in DPN (p < 0.001). Additional benefits included reductions in neuropathic symptoms (NPSI from 61.1 to 11.1; p < 0.001), autonomic symptoms (SAS from 16.5 to 9.9; p = 0.02) and improvements in sleep, functioning, and quality of life (EQ-VAS from 38.8 to 77.9; p < 0.001). Neurological signs remained unchanged. Use of analgesics decreased substantially (59% complete withdrawal; 41% partial), and 96% of patients reported "much" or "very much" improvement. Twelve-month IENFD measurements showed a lower-than-expected mean decline across etiologies, with IENFD increases outnumbering decreases, although the changes were modest. SCS was associated with substantial and durable improvements in pain, neuropathic and autonomic symptoms, and other wellbeing outcomes across multiple painful PPN etiologies. The IENFD results suggest that SCS may have some effects on small-fiber integrity.

papers.title: Psychiatric comorbidities in pediatric epilepsy: a single-center retrospective study highlighting the burden of depressive symptoms.
papers.abstract: Epilepsy in the pediatric population is frequently associated with psychiatric comorbidities. Depression is of particular clinical significance given its elevated incidence and substantial impact on quality of life, treatment adherence, and psychosocial functioning. The prevalence of depression in children with epilepsy ranges from 7% to 14%, considerably higher than the 1-5% reported in the general pediatric population. The relationship between epilepsy and depression appears bidirectional: epilepsy predisposes to depressive disorders, and depression may increase seizure risk, suggesting shared neurobiological pathways. This study aimed to assess the prevalence of psychiatric symptoms in pediatric patients with epilepsy, with particular focus on depressive symptomatology, and to examine associations with etiological and clinical variables. This retrospective study included 240 pediatric patients (aged 2-18 years) diagnosed with epilepsy between 2013 and 2024. Psychiatric symptoms were ascertained retrospectively from clinical records. Patients were categorized into two groups: those with an identified genetic and/or structural abnormality (G1, n = 60) and those without (G2, n = 180). Statistical analysis employed the chi-squared test and Student's t-test (p < 0.05). Psychiatric symptoms were identified in 30% of patients (72/240, 95% CI 24.2-35.8%). The most prevalent disorder was attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD; n = 30), followed by sleep disturbance/asthenia (n = 19), aggression/temper tantrums (n = 13), depressive/mood symptoms (n = 11), anxiety symptoms (n = 10), autism spectrum disorder (n = 6), eating behavior alterations (n = 4), self-harm (n = 4), adjustment/self-esteem features (n = 3), obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD; n = 3), panic attacks (n = 2), and suicide attempts (n = 2). Psychiatric symptoms were significantly more prevalent in G1 (42%, 95% CI 29.2-54.1%) than in G2 (26%, 95% CI 19.7-32.5%; p = 0.03), corresponding to an odds ratio of 2.02 (95% CI 1.10-3.72). No significant associations were found between psychiatric symptoms and age, sex, family history, or treatment regimen. Psychiatric comorbidities, including depressive symptomatology, are common in pediatric epilepsy and likely associated with underlying neurobiological factors. These findings support integrating neuropsychiatric screening, using validated instruments such as the Children's Depression Inventory-2 (CDI-2) and the Neurological Disorders Depression Inventory for Epilepsy-Youth version (NDDI-E-Y), into routine epilepsy care.

papers.title: Modern time-series and spectral methods for analysing solar and stellar oscillatory signals.
papers.abstract: Time-series analysis plays a central role in understanding oscillatory and wave phenomena in solar and stellar atmospheres. However, astrophysical observations are inherently affected by instrumental noise, non-stationary dynamics and uneven sampling. This review provides a comprehensive overview and comparative analysis of principal methods for detecting and characterizing periodicities in solar and stellar signals. We cover Fourier-transform-based transforms, nonlinear fitting-based methods (Lomb-Scargle periodogram (LSP)), time-frequency methods (wavelet and synchrosqueezed transforms) and adaptive decomposition techniques (empirical mode decomposition (EMD)). Advanced statistical significance tests, including false-alarm probability (FAP), autoregressive (AR) models and Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approaches, are discussed alongside their practical limitations and misuse risks. Through comparative analysis using synthetic benchmarks, we provide guidelines for selecting methods based on signal stationarity, sampling regularity and noise characteristics. Finally, we outline future directions that integrate Bayesian inference with time-frequency analysis to achieve both statistical rigour and temporal localization in studying non-stationary solar and stellar oscillations. This article is part of the theme issue 'Transferable mechanisms in the oscillatory processes of solar and stellar flares'.
papers.journal: Philosophical transactions. Series A, Mathematical, physical, and engineering sciences

papers.title: Associations of body composition and chronotype with social jet lag in Brazilian adults: A cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Social jet lag (SJL) refers to the discrepancy between average sleep timing on workdays and free days and has been implicated in weight gain, changes in body composition, and chronotype. This study aimed to examine the association between SJL, body composition parameters, and chronotype. Participants wore an actigraph for 14 consecutive days and completed a socioeconomic questionnaire and the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ). Body composition was assessed by bioelectrical impedance analysis. SJL was calculated as the absolute difference between the midpoint of sleep on weekends and weekdays |SJL = MSweekend - Msweekday|. Data normality was assessed using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, and appropriate parametric or nonparametric tests were applied. Adjusted binary logistic regression models were performed with SJL category (low versus moderate/high) as the dependent variable to investigate associations with body composition and chronotype, adjusting for age, sex, and paid employment. The sample comprised 97 individuals, predominantly female (71.1%). Most participants exhibited low SJL (58.8%) and a morning chronotype (57.3%). In the adjusted analyses, which included 91 participants for body composition variables and 96 for chronotype, participants classified as having increased metabolic risk according to waist-to-hip ratio showed higher odds of moderate/high SJL (OR = 5.86, 95% CI: 1.49-22.99). No clear associations were observed for fat mass, fat-free mass, body fat percentage, BMI, or chronotype. These findings indicate that SJL was associated with waist-to-hip ratio classification in this sample, whereas associations with other body composition parameters and chronotype were not evident.

papers.title: [Discussion on the closed-loop regulation strategy for acupuncture "Deqi" based on brain-computer interface and its peripheral-central mechanisms].
papers.abstract: It is held that "Deqi" is the key to the therapeutic effect of acupuncture, but its evaluation has long relied on subjective feelings and lacks objective biological indicators. In the present article, we systematically review the current research status of brain-computer interface (BCI) technology based on electroencephalogram (EEG) in analyzing the peripheral-cerebral neural mechanism of "Deqi", and further explore how to utilize the closed-loop regulation ability of BCI to actively induce and maintain the "Deqi" state. By integrating domestic and foreign literature, we analyzed the peripheral initiation mechanism and central response characteristics of "Deqi", and explored its application value of EEG-BCI in the objective identification and the construction of closed-loop feedback systems. Studies have demonstrated that EEG, with its millisecond-level time resolution, can capture the dynamic changes of neural oscillations during the "Deqi" process in real time. The feature decoding method based on machine learning further realizes the objective identification of the "Deqi" state, while the closed-loop feedback system constructed by BCI technology provides an innovative path for precise acupuncture treatment. However, this field still faces some challenges such as signal artifact interference, insufficient decoding accuracy, and inconsistent research paradigms. The deep integration of EEG-BCI with acupuncture medicine provides a key technical platform for decoding the scientific connotation of "Deqi" and active regulation. In the future, efforts should be made to develop dynamic network decoding technology, further deepen the research on peripheral-cerebral coupling mechanisms, and promote the transformation of the system towards intelligence and standardization.
papers.journal: Zhen ci yan jiu = Acupuncture research

papers.title: Euploid embryo counts in IVF: Associations with maternal age, vitamin D, sleep quality, and BMI.
papers.abstract: Maternal age is a known correlate of embryo euploidy, but the associations with vitamin D status, sleep quality, and body mass index (BMI) are not fully understood. This study investigated these factors in relation to euploid embryo counts per in vitro fertilization (IVF) cycle. This retrospective cross-sectional study included 42 women undergoing a single IVF cycle with preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy at one center. Serum vitamin D levels, BMI, and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scores were recorded before ovarian stimulation. Analyses involved multivariable linear regression, bootstrapping with 1,000 resamples, sensitivity analysis, and binomial models that accounted for the number of embryos tested. Linear regression revealed negative associations between maternal age and PSQI scores with euploid embryo counts, while vitamin D was positively associated (regression coefficient = 0.055; p = 0.006). BMI was not a significant factor. Vitamin D was the only factor whose bias-corrected and accelerated bootstrap 95% confidence interval excluded zero (0.006-0.145), and its association remained significant in sensitivity analysis. Higher vitamin D levels were also linked to a higher euploidy rate in binomial models (p = 0.017), including models adjusted separately for anti-Müllerian hormone (p = 0.026) or antral follicle count (p = 0.044). Maternal age, BMI, and PSQI scores were not significant in these models. Across all analyses, vitamin D demonstrated the most consistent association with embryo euploidy. These preliminary findings from a small observational cohort warrant confirmation in larger prospective studies and do not establish causality.

papers.title: An interval-based approach to measuring eating jet lag in female healthcare shift workers.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms regulate physiological and metabolic functions, and their disruption, particularly from shift work, is associated with adverse health outcomes such as obesity or cardiovascular disease. Meal timing variability, or eating jet lag, has emerged as a valuable marker of circadian misalignment. This study introduces a novel method to assess eating jet lag through direct comparison of food intake intervals, addressing limitations of traditional midpoint-based approaches reducing intervals to single values, potentially overlooking meaningful overlap. We conducted a cross-sectional study on 290 female healthcare professionals in Asturias, Spain, from a larger cohort of 679 participants with complete temporal data for meals across morning, afternoon, and night shifts. The proposed method calculates the degree of embedding between intake intervals during work shifts and rest days, and a global index is derived by aggregating alignment values across shifts. Results show that the interval-based method captures temporal overlap not represented by the midpoint-based approach, especially where the midpoint method underestimates alignment. Bland-Altman analysis showed systematic and proportional disagreement between the two approaches, with discrepancies greater at lower levels of alignment. This approach provides complementary information for evaluating eating-window alignment and provides a basis for future studies between eating-window alignment and health-related outcomes.

papers.title: Interferon-γ Mitigates Oxaliplatin-Induced Neurotoxicity: Analogies With Connexin 43.
papers.abstract: Chemotherapy-induced neuropathy is a major side effect of platinum-based drugs such as oxaliplatin. Given the context-dependent pro-inflammatory or neuroprotective actions of interferon-γ (IFN-γ), this study investigated its role in an in vitro model of oxaliplatin-induced neurotoxicity (OIPN). Rat organotypic spinal cord slices were exposed to oxaliplatin to model chemotherapy-induced neurotoxicity responses in vitro. IFN-γ cytotoxicity was assessed at 6 and 24 h. Neurotoxicity, inflammatory mediators, neurotrophic factors, and markers of glial and neuronal activation were analyzed by biochemical and immunohistochemical assays. Connexin 43 (Cx43) was assessed using Gap19 and Gap27 to probe hemichannel and gap-junction contributions. Electrophysiological recordings characterized neuronal excitability. IFN-γ (6.5-200 ng/mL) was non-toxic and, at 65 ng/mL, significantly reduced oxaliplatin-induced neurotoxicity, decreasing LDH release and suppressing pro-inflammatory mediators (CCL2, SerpinA3N, CGRP, substance P, c-Fos). IFN-γ modulated its signaling by reducing IFNγR and increasing IRF1 expression. It prevented oxaliplatin-induced overexpression of neurotrophic factors and reduced glial and neuronal hyperactivation markers, preserving neuronal integrity. IFN-γ reduced Cx43 expression and hemichannel activity, and Gap19 reproduced selected protective effects. Electrophysiology showed attenuation of oxaliplatin-induced neuronal hyperexcitability. IFN-γ attenuates oxaliplatin-induced neurotoxic responses in an in vitro spinal cord model. The parallel reduction in Cx43 expression and hemichannel activity supports further investigation of Cx43 signaling as a candidate pharmacological target in OIPN.

papers.title: Pah in the era of obesity: navigating phenotypes of pulmonary hypertension.
papers.abstract: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progressive vasculopathy whose phenotype has shifted over the decades from young women to older patients with cardiometabolic comorbidities. Obesity is among the most prevalent and clinically consequential of these comorbidities, affecting 24-40% of patients in contemporary PAH registries. We review the epidemiology of obesity and its impact on PAH; the definition of obesity and the limitations of body mass index; the effects of obesity on adipose, cardiovascular and respiratory systems; its association with health disparities; the clinical approach to the patient with obesity and suspected pulmonary hypertension (PH), including right heart catheterization with provocative maneuvers and esophageal manometry; comorbid conditions and the obesity paradox; and management, including weight loss, PAH-specific therapy, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and sleep-disordered breathing. A literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE was performed for articles published from database inception to September 2026. Obesity has implications in the origin, symptoms, diagnosis and management of PH. Accurate characterization of PH in obese patients depends first on measuring and reporting pressures that reflect true transmural hemodynamics. Incretin-based therapy and activin signaling inhibition are promising therapeutic directions, but dedicated trials in patients with obesity and pulmonary hypertension are needed.
