papers.title: Brain NaV1.5 fine-tunes neuronal excitability to facilitate female-directed social behavior in male mice.
papers.abstract: The voltage-gated sodium channel NaV1.5, an essential subtype for cardiac action potential generation, is also enriched in limbic regions of the brain, but its function in the central nervous system remains poorly understood. We performed RNAscope, immunostaining, electrophysiology, fiber photometry, Scn5a knockdown, and behavioral testing to dissect the functional role of NaV1.5 in the brain. NaV1.5 channels are enriched in neurons of posterior bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNSTp) and accumulated at the axon initial segment. Activation of these tetrodotoxin-resistant channels lowers action potential threshold and accelerates spike initiation at relatively hyperpolarized levels of membrane potential (Vm). In vivo fiber photometry showed that BNSTp NaV1.5-expressing neurons in male mice were recruited by salient social stimuli and exhibited hyperpolarizing Vm dynamics during social contacts. Scn5a knockdown selectively attenuated neuronal responses to female chemosensory cues, and disrupted sex preference and female-directed behaviors. These findings identify NaV1.5 as a Vm state-dependent regulator of BNSTp neuronal excitability, and reveal an unexpected role of this channel subtype in female-cue processing and female-directed social behavior in males.

papers.title: Statistical Learning of Feature-Spatial Mappings and Its Modulation by Cue-Induced Expectation.
papers.abstract: Visual statistical learning enables individuals to extract regularities from the environment, thereby optimizing attentional allocation. Previous research has mainly focused on unidimensional location or feature probability learning, leaving unclear whether individuals can acquire multidimensional mappings between target features and high-probability spatial locations, and how cue-induced expectations modulate the neural expression of such mappings. We employed a location probability paradigm combined with multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) and recorded EEG. Reaction times showed a significant gradient from the feature-matched high-probability location to the low-probability location, indicating successful acquisition of feature-spatial mappings under both cue conditions. The N2pc did not reliably differentiate the two high-probability location conditions, providing no detectable evidence of feature-dependent modulation of early lateralized selection. Predictive cues elicited brief pretarget alpha lateralization toward the cue-associated HPTL. Search-array-locked MVPA discriminated feature-matched from feature-mismatched HPTL trials under both cue conditions, with stronger decoding under predictive cueing. These findings show that learned feature-spatial regularities were expressed behaviorally and in distributed neural activity, and that predictive cues modulated their neural expression before and after search-array onset.

papers.title: From Polycystic Ovary Syndrome to Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome: A Practical Clinical Review.
papers.abstract: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS), recently renamed Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS), is the most common endocrine disorder affecting women of reproductive age. The new nomenclature reflects growing recognition that this condition extends far beyond ovarian dysfunction, encompassing complex endocrine, metabolic, cardiovascular, and psychological abnormalities. Although the diagnostic criteria remain unchanged, the name change emphasizes the multisystem nature of the disorder and may improve disease recognition and patient care. This review provides a practical, evidence-based overview of the diagnosis and management of PMOS/PCOS, highlighting recent updates from the 2023 International Evidence-Based Guideline. We discuss the evaluation of hyperandrogenism and ovulatory dysfunction in reproductive-aged women, as well as the assessment and treatment of obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, obstructive sleep apnea, and mental health disorders. Finally, we summarize current pharmacological therapies and emerging treatment strategies, highlighting key knowledge gaps that must be bridged to optimize long-term cardiometabolic and reproductive outcomes.
papers.journal: The American journal of the medical sciences

papers.title: Influence of chiropractic care on sleep-related behavior of athletic Mangalarga Marchador horses.
papers.abstract: Sleep is a fundamental biological process for homeostasis in mammals. Chiropractic is a manual therapeutic approach that aims to restore joint mobility, correct biomechanical dysfunctions, and optimize welfare. The present study examined the influence of chiropractic sessions on resting behavior patterns of Mangalarga Marchador horses raised in an intensive system. Nine Mangalarga Marchador horses, with an average age of 4.2 ± 1.2 years, were evaluated for their sleep-related behavior over 72 hours, followed by a chiropractic session, and reassessed over the next 72 hours post-session. After 35 days, horses received a second chiropractic session and were observed for another 72 hours, pre- and post-session. There was a reduction in wakefulness time (Pre: 1,128.22±32.02; Post: 1,063.66±29.16 min, p=0.003) and an increase in time in lateral recumbency after the chiropractic sessions (1st: from 129.24±43.88 min to 147.14±46.25 min and 2nd: from 88.55±28.19 min to 143.10±38.58 min, p=0.004). These results suggest that chiropractic care is associated with changes in sleep-related behavior in athletic horses. Further studies using electroencephalography are needed to determine whether these behavioral changes are associated with alterations in sleep physiology.

papers.title: EEG-VTSFN: An enhanced approach for differentiating between unipolar and bipolar mood disorders.
papers.abstract: Accurate differentiation between Bipolar Disorder (BD) and Unipolar Depression (UD) is a significant clinical challenge due to overlapping manifestations and a lack of objective biomarkers. While EEG offers high temporal resolution, its psychiatric utility for diagnostic differentiation remains limited. To address this, we propose the Variational Autoencoder (VAE)-based Time-Space Fusion Network (VTSFN). VTSFN transforms complex EEG signals into latent-space representations to mitigate noise and construct stable latent co-activation patterns. By integrating Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and attention mechanisms, the model captures temporal dynamics to identify discriminative patterns. Our results demonstrate that VTSFN achieved the highest accuracy and AUC point estimates among the evaluated models, with a test-set accuracy of 79.3% (95% CI, 65.5%-93.1%) and an AUC of 82.7% (95% CI, 63.2%-98.5%), without significant paired AUC differences at p < 0.01. Validation in a diagnostic-switch (tBD) cohort (n = 22) identified 17/22 converters (sensitivity, 77.3%; 95% CI, 59.1%-90.9%), requiring further longitudinal validation. Exploratory feature analysis revealed that, compared with UD patients, BD and tBD patients exhibited weaker latent co-activation in right parieto-temporal and temporo-occipital regions, alongside stronger latent co-activation in left frontal-right parietal and temporal regions. These model-derived channel similarity patterns require independent validation.

papers.title: Co-developmental trajectories of internalizing symptoms and psychotic-like experiences among adolescents: The predictive role of sleep disturbance.
papers.abstract: Internalizing symptoms and psychotic-like experiences (PLEs) are common among adolescents. However, few studies have explored the longitudinal co-development of internalizing symptoms and PLEs in this age group. A total of 7529 adolescents (M age at baseline = 13.89 years, SD = 1.34; 50% girls) participated in this three-wave longitudinal study. A parallel-process latent class growth analysis identified joint trajectories of internalizing symptoms and PLEs, and multinomial logistic regression examined the effect of sleep disturbance. Three distinct trajectories were identified: a low-risk group (74.0%), a pure-internalizing symptoms group (13.5%), and a chronic co-occurring group (12.5%). After controlling for sample characteristics, negative life events during follow-up, and sleep duration, baseline sleep disturbance was significantly associated with both the pure-internalizing symptoms trajectory (OR = 3.41, 95% CI = 2.84-4.08) and the chronic co-occurring trajectory (OR = 3.69, 95% CI = 3.06-4.46). These findings indicate that sleep disturbance independently associated with the heterogeneous co-developmental trajectories of internalizing symptoms and PLEs. Early assessment and treatment of sleep disturbance may be an important strategy for the prevention and intervention of psychopathology development.

papers.title: Towards semantic brain-computer interfacing: The graded inventory of semantic triggers (GIST) paradigm.
papers.abstract: Semantic Brain-Computer Interfaces (sBCIs) aim to decode conceptual information directly from neural activity, enabling more efficient and natural communication for individuals with severe motor impairments. However, existing approaches are often confounded by stimulus-driven perceptual processes and lack a reliable means of tagging the moment of concept formation. We introduce the Graded Inventory of Semantic Triggers (GIST), a novel electroencephalography (EEG) paradigm designed to elicit semantic retrieval from graded verbal clues with precise temporal alignment.Approach: EEG data were recorded from 14 participants performing the GIST task across three semantic categories (food, musical instruments, and body parts). Target neural activity was aligned to each participant's self-reported moment of semantic retrieval (spacebar press), enabling response-locked analysis. Here, we propose a staged framework where the first comprises a Conformer-based encoder trained on pooled data using a hybrid contrastive objective that combines instance-level consistency and cross-participant class alignment with domain-adversarial learning to reduce participant-specific information. In the second stage, the frozen encoder is transferred to a held-out participant whose data played no part in Stage 1, and a support vector machine is calibrated on that participant's own labelled items under a nested leave-one-item-out protocol.Results: Above-chance semantic decoding was achieved in all three pairwise tasks. Mean accuracies were 73.4% (Body vs. Food), 70.7% (Body vs. Music), and 68.2% (Food vs. Music). Participant-level permutation tests were significant in 9/11 participants for Body vs. Food and 8/11 for each of the other tasks (p < 0.05). The pre-response interval at [-1.5s, -0.5s] was the most discriminative.Significance: The GIST paradigm enables controlled elicitation and temporal alignment of semantic processing while reducing perceptual confounds. Combined with cross-participant representation pretraining and participant-specific calibration, the results demonstrate above-chance decoding of semantic categories from EEG in individuals excluded from representation learning, supporting the feasibility of sBCIs.

papers.title: ACF-Net: Design of an adaptive cross-modal fusion network for cross-subject wearable EEG-EMG gesture recognition.
papers.abstract: Cross-subject gesture recognition in wearable brain-computer interfaces is constrained by four structural deficiencies: symmetric cross-modal attention discarding cortical precedence over muscular execution, priors confined to post hoc analysis, invariance anchored on unimodal features, and adaptation requiring labelled target-domain data. This study closes these gaps by embedding corticomuscular coupling directly into the network architecture rather than recovering it from data.Approach: ACF-Net is a four-stage pipeline embedding neurophysiological priors directly into fusion. The corticomuscular coherence prior injection layer (CMC-Prior) encodes time-lagged coherence and phase-locking values for every electroencephalography (EEG)-electromyography (EMG) channel pair as a learnable bias tensor. Granger-causality-inspired directed cross-modal attention (GC-Attn) uses a causal mask allowing only EEG-to-EMG influence within 30-120 ms. The fused embedding is projected onto a symmetric positive definite manifold with log-Euclidean triplet loss. Physiology-consistent test-time adaptation (PC-TTA) updates only batch-normalisation affine parameters, using EEG-precedes-EMG as unlabelled self-supervision, eliminating labelled target data. Leave-one-subject-out validation on WAY-EEG-GAL (12 participants) and WEE-Ges (20 participants, three days) used fold-wise priors and Holm-corrected Wilcoxon tests.Main results: ACF-Net reached 87.6% on WAY-EEG-GAL and 89.2% on WEE-Ges, exceeding the strongest baseline by 9.4 and 9.1 percentage points with all comparisons significant after correction. Ablation attributed gains of 6.3, 4.9, 3.4 and 1.8 percentage points to directed attention, prior injection, manifold embedding and test-time adaptation. Accuracy remained 77.5% under 20 mm simulated electrode displacement, adaptation reduced the cross-day loss from 6.8 to 2.1 percentage points, and a forward pass on an NVIDIA Jetson Nano took 32.4 ms within a 178 ms end-to-end response at 30.9 Hz. Significance: Learned coupling weights recovered central-to-forearm-extensor projection, and delays matched corticospinal conduction with motor-unit recruitment, suggesting physiological structure, not dataset-specific statistics. Yet healthy young adults, gel-based/semi-dry wired hardware, and simulated displacement make this methodological; clinical and wireless dry-electrode transfer remains unestablished.

papers.title: Exploratory heart rate variability patterns across sleep stages following a 7-day multicomponent mantra-based cognitive intervention: A pilot randomized pre-post controlled study.
papers.abstract: Cognitive-contemplative practices could potentially affect autonomic function, but existing research has focused on waking measures of heart rate variability (HRV). It remains unclear whether changes associated with brief interventions differ across sleep stages. To determine whether differences in HRV according to sleep stage would differ in a group undergoing a 7-day, multicomponent, Hare Krishna mantra-based cognitive therapy (HMBCT) intervention compared to a group engaging in their normal routine activities. Thirty-four healthy males aged 18-30 years were randomized to HMBCT (n = 17) or a usual-routine control condition (n = 17). Overnight polysomnography with continuous ECG was conducted at baseline and after the 7-day intervention period. HRV variables were calculated using time-domain and Poincaré/geometric HRV indices separately for REM, N2, and N3 sleep stages. Group × Time interactions were analyzed using repeated measures ANOVA, and then subjected to Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction in 30 primary tests. Nine interactions reached the nominal uncorrected threshold (p < .05): four in REM (SDNN, RMSSD, SD1, SD2) and five in N2 (SDNN, RMSSD, pNN50, SD1, CVI), while none did so in N3. Effect sizes of REM/N2 interaction were estimated as partial η2p = 0.120-0.173. However, none remained statistically significant after FDR correction (smallest q = 0.148). Nominal interactions were more pronounced in REM and N2 sleep stages, but none of the primary interactions survived multiple testing correction. Thus the results are exploratory and should be confirmed in other studies.

papers.title: Morning lighting intervention reduces fatigue and improves sleep in Parkinson disease.
papers.abstract: Fatigue and sleep disturbances are common in Parkinson Disease (PD) and significantly reduce quality of life, yet effective pharmacological treatments are limited. Light therapy offers a promising non-pharmacologic approach, but most lighting interventions have focused on improving sleep. Using a novel and easily administered morning lighting intervention, we previously demonstrated improvement in sleep duration. We have now extended the prior study through the addition of 23 individuals to investigate the intervention's effect on fatigue and sleep. In this single-arm intervention study, participants received morning light for 4 consecutive weeks from table or floor luminaires designed to deliver circadian-effective ambient light at home. Objective sleep was measured with wrist-worn actigraphy and subjective sleep, fatigue and mood were assessed using standardized questionnaires. Analysis of pre and post intervention data for the current cohort was performed separately as well as in combination with the 20 participants from the previously reported pilot study. For the 23 current participants, fatigue on the Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy-Fatigue (FACIT-F) scale improved by 3.9 ± 1.00 points (p = 0.0026). While sleep duration increased by mean 21.3 ± 14.4 min, it was not statistically significant (p = 0.082). When combined with the 20 participants from the prior pilot study, significant improvement in fatigue by 2.8 ± 0.85 points (p = 0.0033) was observed and sleep duration was also significantly increased by 24.7 ± 10.4 min (p = 0.012). These findings support morning light as a novel intervention for fatigue in PD.
papers.journal: Neurotherapeutics : the journal of the American Society for Experimental NeuroTherapeutics

papers.title: A fungal clock protein exerts extra-circadian roles in nitrogen metabolism and mitochondrial function.
papers.abstract: Protein moonlighting refers to functions in polypeptides exceeding those considered canonical roles. While this vision is changing our understanding of cellular signaling integration, in timekeeping proteins this duality, if any, remains mostly unexplored. Circadian clocks are widespread cellular machineries that converge on shared architectural principles, built around negative feedback loops involving the activity of pacemaker proteins. In fungi, FREQUENCY (FRQ) is the defining timeteller, but whether it has roles outside the clock is unknown. Here, we show that the FRQ protein of the fungal phytopathogen Botrytis cinerea also operates as a clock-independent metabolic hub. Loss of FRQ results in the inability to release Nitrogen Catabolite Repression, while the loss-of-function mutant accumulates elevated reactive oxygen species and exhibits sensitivity to mitochondria-targeting fungicides. Secondary metabolite profiles are also largely altered. Together, our findings establish that a core clock protein moonlights as a metabolic integrator, independent of its clock function, raising the question of whether metabolic scaffolding represents an underappreciated role of circadian pacemaker proteins.

papers.title: When brain networks crash: connectivity, slow-wave activity and neural replay in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: Brain connectivity disruption is a hallmark of neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet how network breakdown gives rise to cognitive deficits remains unclear. Here, we review the evidence bearing on three interconnected processes that have been proposed to link molecular pathology to cognitive decline. First, we summarize evidence that misfolded proteins propagate along brain connectivity pathways, making the connectome the biological substrate for disease progression. Second, we discuss the divergent trajectory reported across the AD continuum, an initial compensatory hyperconnectivity followed by progressive hypoconnectivity and network collapse, together with the accompanying oscillatory changes (intrusion of slow-wave activity and suppression of fast oscillatory rhythms). Third, we examine the proposal that these oscillatory alterations compromise neural replay mechanisms, critical for memory consolidation, representing the potential link between network dysfunction and cognitive decline. By integrating evidence from human neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and animal models in the AD field, this framework offers new perspectives for therapeutic interventions targeting brain connectivity and replay mechanisms in neurodegenerative diseases.

papers.title: Characteristics of Women Ages 40-60 with Menopausal Symptoms: United States, 2025.
papers.abstract: The menopausal transition is a critical window for the health of women and may serve as an inflection point for the onset of chronic disease. During this transition, a woman's ovaries become less efficient at producing estrogen and progesterone, and women may experience symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, insomnia or sleep disturbances, and abnormal uterine bleeding. This report describes demographic and geographic characteristics of women ages 40-60 who had menopausal symptoms in the past 12 months using data from the 2025 National Health Interview Survey (NHIS). Estimates of current prescription medication use for menopausal symptoms by age are also provided. NHIS is a nationally representative household survey of the civilian, non-institutionalized U.S. population. Point estimates and the corresponding confidence intervals for this analysis were calculated using SAS-callable SUDAAN software to account for the complex sample design of NHIS. In 2025, nearly one in two women (49.4%) ages 40-60 who were not currently pregnant, postpartum, or in surgical menopause reported menopausal symptoms in the past 12 months. The presence of symptoms varied by age, race and ethnicity, educational attainment, and urbanization level. Women ages 48-51 (62.0%) and 52-55 (67.4%) were the most likely to report menopausal symptoms compared with younger and older women. Among women who reported menopausal symptoms in the past 12 months, 15.6% indicated that they were currently taking a prescription medication for those symptoms. Of these women, prescription use was highest among women ages 52-55 and 56-60.

papers.title: Restless legs syndrome and other neurological disorders: A systematic-narrative hybrid literature review with exploratory meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Restless legs syndrome (RLS) is a sleep-related sensorimotor disorder affecting approximately 3% of adults worldwide. This review aims to synthesize current evidence on associations between RLS and major neurological conditions, provide an exploratory quantitative synthesis summarizing association patterns and heterogeneity, and identify priority mechanistic and clinical research gaps. Databases were searched from inception until August 2026. In our exploratory synthesis of 119 unique studies, RLS was significantly associated with Parkinson's disease (case-control OR 3.22, 95% CI 2.35-4.41; cohort RR 1.74, 95% CI 1.02-2.95), multiple sclerosis (OR 4.04, 95% CI 3.26-5.00), neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (OR 2.91, 95% CI 1.45-5.84), migraine or headache disorders (forward OR 2.72, 95% CI 2.19-3.38; reverse adjusted OR 1.53, 95% CI 1.36-1.73), peripheral neuropathy (OR 3.82, 95% CI 2.49-5.83), epilepsy (OR 2.11, 95% CI 1.58-2.82), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (OR 7.69, 95% CI 2.74-21.59). This work is an evidence-mapping review with exploratory pooling and is not intended as a definitive evidence synthesis. RLS is likely associated with neurodegenerative and other specific neurological conditions. Recognition of these associations may support earlier identification of comorbid conditions and targeted management strategies. However, the current evidence remains observational and heterogeneous.

papers.title: Delayed school start-times and adolescent sleep duration: A systematic umbrella review.
papers.abstract: Expert panels have long recommended delayed school start-times (SSTs) as necessary for addressing widespread adolescent sleep loss; nevertheless, adoption of recommendations has been slow. The major goals of this umbrella review were to explore the consistency of review teams' recommendations while describing and assessing review quality. We used systematic procedures to identify five meta-analyses and four narrative reviews. Authors of all nine reviews concluded that adolescent sleep duration (ASD) likely increased when SSTs were later but usually recommended limited adoption. Reviewers' hesitancy to recommend widespread adoption reflected (a) the modest average sleep gains reported in two reviews that met all AMSTAR2 critical criteria for producing sound estimates of effectiveness, (b) the lack of evidence that gains in sleep were sustained, and (c) the limited quality of primary studies. Potential moderating factors (e.g., students' background, school type and size) were explored but little progress was made due to missing data; however geographic location was identified as a potential moderator of SSTs' impact on ASD. Our results support the need for well-controlled local studies of SST delays that are guided by standard reporting protocols. We also recommend needs assessments to capture local sleep norms and unique community conditions. Registration: PROSPERO CRD42023373423.

papers.title: Predictors of residual obstructive sleep apnea after mandibular distraction osteogenesis in infants with Pierre Robin sequence: Insight on syndromic stratification.
papers.abstract: Mandibular distraction osteogenesis (MDO) improves obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in infants with Pierre Robin sequence (PRS), but residual disease is common. We sought to identify predictors of residual severe OSA after MDO. We performed a retrospective cohort study of infants with PRS who underwent MDO and postoperative polysomnography (PSG) at a tertiary pediatric center between 2019 and 2025. Residual severe OSA was defined a priori as postoperative obstructive apnea-hypopnea index (oAHI) > 10 events/hour or postoperative need for a tracheostomy. Candidate predictors were evaluated using univariate logistic regression. Stickler syndrome was analyzed both within and excluded from the syndromic category based on its tongue-base airway physiology resembling isolated PRS. Thirty-three infants met inclusion criteria, of whom 11 (33.3%) had residual severe OSA; one required tracheostomy. Syndromic diagnosis excluding Stickler syndrome (odds ratio [OR] 5.95, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.22-28.95, p = 0.03), neurologic hypotonia (OR = 5.40, 95%CI 1.08-26.93, p = 0.04) and higher preoperative oAHI (OR = 1.04 per event/hour, 95%CI 1.01-1.07, p = 0.02) were associated with residual severe OSA. Exploratory receiver operating characteristic analysis demonstrated modest discrimination (AUC = 0.70, 95%CI 0.43-0.97) with an optimal preoperative oAHI cutoff of 96 events/hour (50% sensitivity, 95% specificity). Among 25 infants with paired PSGs, median oAHI reduction was similar between the non-syndromic/Stickler and syndromic groups (90.5% vs 87.6%, p = 0.3). One-third of infants had residual severe OSA after MDO. Higher preoperative oAHI, neurologic hypotonia, and syndromic diagnosis excluding Stickler syndrome were associated with residual disease and may help identify infants who warrant closer postoperative PSG surveillance.

papers.title: The unique contributions of negative emotionality and sleep problems to toddlers' physiological stress response.
papers.abstract: Previous research has examined temperament and sleep separately with respect to their relationship to young children's physiological stress response; however, little research has jointly investigated these two constructs in relation to children's physiological stress response. Previous research also has not considered the potential contributions of individual components of children's negative emotionality to their stress response. In the present study, mothers reported on children's negative emotionality and sleep problems when children were 18 and 24 months old respectively. When children were 30 months old, saliva samples were collected prior to and after the stranger approach task to assess physiological stress response as measured by total cortisol secretion (AUCg) and cortisol reactivity (AUCi). Results showed that frustration was positively associated with AUCg. Frustration and sleep problems were also both positively associated with AUCi, and shyness was negatively associated with AUCi. No other dimensions of negative emotionality were related to AUCg or AUCi. These results highlight the unique contributions of toddlers' temperament and sleep difficulties to their stress physiology. Furthermore, these results highlight the importance of parsing out the individual components of negative emotionality when conducting temperament research on children's stress response.

papers.title: Sleep in the first three years of life: Age-related patterns and predictors in a South African sample.
papers.abstract: Sleep is integral to early neurodevelopment and health, yet most normative data derive from high-income, global North populations. Context-specific data from sub-Saharan Africa, and South Africa in particular, remain scarce. This study describes sleep patterns across the first three years of life in a South African sample and examines caregiver and child characteristics associated with variation in sleep outcomes. A cross-sectional online survey was completed by 340 South African caregivers of children aged 0-36 months. Sleep was assessed using items from the Brief Infant Sleep Questionnaire-Revised. Several sleep outcomes were examined across six age bands. One-way ANOVAs examined age-related differences, and multiple linear regression analyses identified caregiver and child correlates of sleep. Significant age-related differences were observed for total sleep duration, nighttime consolidation, and daytime sleep, with large effect sizes for daytime sleep. Bedtime, bedtime consistency, and sleep onset latency remained similar across the six age groups (0-3-25-36 months). Child age was the most consistent predictor of sleep outcomes. Caregiver unemployment was associated with shorter and less consolidated nighttime sleep. Second-born or later children showed more frequent night wakings and greater daytime napping. Intermediate temperament was associated with longer sleep onset latency. Age-related differences in sleep patterns during the first three years are broadly consistent with international findings, though aspects of sleep timing appear more contextually shaped. Findings provide preliminary data for South Africa and highlight the need for age-stratified, culturally sensitive sleep guidance and interventions.

papers.title: Assisting Screening of Adolescent Depression With Large Language Models as Symptom Detectors: Algorithm Development and Validation.
papers.abstract: Depression prevalence is rising in adolescents and young adults (ages 10-24 years). Traditional screening methods for depression, such as the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9), are particularly challenging for adolescents. AI has potential to help with this, but the scarcity of annotated datasets highlights the need for off-the-shelf approaches. In this study, we investigate the feasibility of using state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) to detect depressive symptoms in adolescent settings (ages 15-17 years). This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility of using in-context learning with LLMs to identify depressive symptoms in free-text clinical notes for adolescent populations, to evaluate the feasibility of off-the-shelf LLM configurations in detecting PHQ-9 symptom-related information under zero- and few-shot settings, and to demonstrate the potential clinical utility of LLM-driven evidence extraction through an interpretable AI-based depression screening tool. We examined free text of the electronic health records (EHRs) of adolescent patients with the diagnosis of depression or related mood disorders (age groups 15-17 years, 924 patients) from the Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center. We leveraged the combination of the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) and the PHQ-9 to develop tailored categories suited for adolescent depression symptoms. We applied 3 state-of-the-art LLMs (Llama, smaller FLAN-T5, and Phi) to identify these symptom categories in zero- and few-shot configurations, allowing us to assess their performance without additional task-specific training. A word-search model was used as the baseline comparator. We manually annotated clinical notes for 22 patients across 16 depression-related symptom categories. Our analysis shows that all LLMs substantially outperformed the word-matching baseline. Within the evaluated prompting configurations, FLAN-T5 achieved the highest precision (average F1-score=0.65, precision=0.78) and strong performance in detecting rare symptoms such as sleep problems (F1-score=0.92) and self-loathing (F1-score=0.80). Phi offered a balanced performance (precision=0.44, recall=0.60), while Llama 3 achieved the highest recall (0.90) but tended to overgeneralize, making it less suitable for precise screening. Within this pilot study, the best-performing LLM exceeded the baseline F1-score by 0.43. Finally, we demonstrate the clinical utility of FLAN-T5 annotations as features in a machine learning model, which distinguished depression cases from controls with high precision (0.78). We used a range of popular LLMs to identify indicators of adolescent (ages 15-17 years) depression symptoms in mental health notes. Within the evaluated configurations, FLAN-T5 demonstrated the most favorable balance between precision and recall. These results support the feasibility of using off-the-shelf LLMs for symptom detection in adolescent clinical notes, while future work using standardized prompting strategies and task formulations will help establish more definitive comparisons between model architectures. The computational efficiency of FLAN-T5 further supports its potential for deployment in resource-limited clinical settings. Our findings require further validation for broader populations and other mental health conditions.

papers.title: Sleep Quality as a Mediator Between Digital Competence and Online Exam Anxiety Among Nursing Students.
papers.abstract: Nursing students increasingly have online examinations, which can provoke significant anxiety. Digital competence, the ability to confidently and critically use digital technologies for learning and professional practice, has become essential for navigating these digital assessment environments; yet, its relationship with exam anxiety remains underexplored. This study examined whether sleep quality mediates and/or moderates the relationship between digital competence and online exam anxiety among nursing students. A cross-sectional descriptive correlational design was used with 597 undergraduate nursing students. Participants completed the Students' Digital Competence Scale, the Test Anxiety Scale for Online Exams, and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. Mediation and moderation analyses were conducted using the PROCESS macro for SPSS (models 4 and 1) with bootstrapping. Digital competence showed a significant total effect on online exam anxiety (B = -0.11, P = .004). After including sleep quality, the direct effect became nonsignificant (B = -0.05, P = .188), whereas the indirect effect through sleep quality was significant, confirming full mediation (B = -0.06, 95% CI [-0.093, -0.034]). Sleep quality did not moderate the relationship (interaction B = -0.01, P = .316). Sleep quality fully mediated but did not moderate the relationship between digital competence and online exam anxiety. Higher digital competence was associated with better sleep quality and lower anxiety. Interventions should integrate digital skills training with sleep hygiene education.

papers.title: Neurosteroids Inhibit RORγ and Induce Major Rearrangement of Its Activation Motif.
papers.abstract: A subset of endogenous steroids can be formed in the brain and exhibit brain-specific activities linked to neuronal health and disease. Despite the biological relevance of these so-called neurosteroids, molecular profiling of their effects is incomplete and their signature in the nuclear hormone receptor family that mediates signals of classical steroid hormones is elusive. Here, we present a comprehensive characterization of neurosteroids for nuclear receptor modulation and reveal pronounced inverse RORγ agonism as a relevant molecular mechanism of several abundant neurosteroids, with an impact on circadian rhythms and transcriptomic profiles in cellular settings. Structural analysis of the DHEA-RORγ interaction demonstrated orthosteric binding and pronounced rearrangements in the RORγ ligand binding domain to a fully repressed state, rationalizing the strong inverse agonist efficacy.

papers.title: Sleep health and uterine leiomyomata incidence and growth: a prospective ultrasound study.
papers.abstract: Poor sleep may negatively impact reproductive outcomes, yet its role in uterine leiomyomata (UL) development has not been studied. We estimated prospectively the association of self-reported sleep health with ultrasound-detected UL incidence and growth in the Study of Environment, Lifestyle, and Fibroids, a prospective cohort of Black individuals aged 23-35 years in Detroit, Michigan. At each of five clinic visits (2010-2020), participants reported sleep duration, frequency of trouble sleeping, and sleep quality, and underwent transvaginal ultrasound to detect incident UL. We used Cox proportional hazards regression models to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and applied inverse probability weights to adjust for time-dependent confounding. Among 1,137 participants, 351 developed UL (10-year cumulative incidence: 30.9%). Short (<6 hours/day, HR=0.30 95% CI: 0.17, 0.55) sleep duration and consistently poorer sleep quality (<4 days/week feeling well-rested, HR=0.78, 95% CI: 0.56, 1.08) were associated with lower UL incidence. Increased frequency of trouble sleeping was positively associated with UL incidence (≥15 days/month, HR=1.96, 95% CI: 0.76, 5.09). Sleep health was not associated with UL growth. In this prospective ultrasound study, sleep measures were inconsistently associated with UL incidence and not associated with UL growth.

papers.title: Motor Expertise Differentiates the Representational Structure of Graded Error Monitoring in Midfrontal Theta.
papers.abstract: Error monitoring has been widely characterized as a graded process that scales with the magnitude of prediction errors. Yet it remains unclear whether this rule is fixed or can be reshaped by expertise. Using a graded-deviation paradigm in table tennis experts and novices, we examined how long-term training refines the neural coding of prediction-outcome discrepancies. Experts demonstrated higher accuracy and stability as deviation angles increased (from 0° to 30°). EEG analyses revealed that frontal-midline theta power scaled with deviation magnitude in both groups but exhibited distinct representational structures: experts showed a three-step graded organization, whereas novices displayed a binary pattern. Multivariate decoding further confirmed that only the frontal-midline region carried discriminable information about error magnitude, with decoding accuracy significantly higher in experts. These findings suggest that expertise is associated with differences in the gain structure of error coding, with experts showing a more parametric mapping of prediction-outcome discrepancies. Frontal-midline theta thus provides a neural substrate for expertise-dependent tuning of predictive precision, indicating that graded error monitoring differs between individuals with different levels of motor expertise.

papers.title: Specific effects of Pulsed Field Ablation on the cardiac tissue, the nervous system and the conduction system in experimental and clinical studies.
papers.abstract: Pulsed field ablation (PFA) has emerged as a novel ablation modality for the treatment of cardiac arrhythmias and has rapidly reshaped contemporary electrophysiology practice. This article provides a comprehensive analysis on the mechanisms underlying the specific effects of PFA on myocardial, neural tissue structures, and the cardiac conduction system, integrating biophysical principles with preclinical and clinical evidence relevant to contemporary electrophysiology practice. This document provides an exhaustive mechanistic explanation for the preferential effects of PFA on myocardium and the limits of the 'tissue-selectivity' concept. The complex interplay between cellular and tissue-level biophysics, biological responses, and tissue regenerative capacity that determines differential susceptibility to electroporation across tissues is analysed. Distinct patterns of lesion formation and maturation following PFA are also reviewed, highlighting the temporal and histopathological differences compared with radiofrequency ablation. Additionally, lesion formation in heterogeneous substrates is analysed, including fibrotic and adipose-rich myocardium, where local electric field distribution critically influences lesion durability. The article further examines the interaction between pulsed electric fields and neural tissue, with emphasis on the phrenic nerve and intrinsic cardiac autonomic nervous system. While nerve stimulation and transient reversible conduction disturbances produced by reversible electroporation can occur during ablation, permanent neural injury appears extremely rare in current clinical experience. Finally, this manuscript examines current understanding regarding the specific effects of PFA on the cardiac conduction system, which according to the limited available evidence appear strongly dependent on electric field dose and anatomical proximity.

papers.title: Safety considerations and clinical monitoring during pulsed field ablation.
papers.abstract: Pulsed field ablation (PFA) has emerged as a transformative technology in cardiac electrophysiology, offering a potentially superior safety profile compared with thermal ablation due to its non-thermal mechanism of irreversible electroporation. Clinical experience confirms a substantial reduction in traditional complications such as pulmonary vein stenosis, atrio-oesophageal fistula, and permanent phrenic nerve injury, though PFA introduces a distinct spectrum of physiologic effects requiring consideration. Coronary vasospasm is the most characteristic phenomenon, ranging from transient, subclinical constriction to rare ischaemic or arrhythmic events; mitigation relies on coronary anatomical awareness, optimized lesion placement, and prophylactic vasodilators. Haemolysis, caused by red blood cell electroporation, varies with catheter design and pulse burden and is typically mild, though high exposure and inadequate hydration may rarely lead to acute kidney injury. Silent cerebral lesions could result from procedural and/or energy-related factors, including gas formation, air ingress, catheter manipulation, and anticoagulation management, with uncertain long-term clinical impact but opportunities for technique-driven reduction. Interactions between PFA and cardiac implantable electronic devices are system- and context-dependent, with monopolar configurations and catheter-lead proximity influencing the risk of transient interference and rare permanent damage.

papers.title: Pulsed field ablation: from concepts to technology.
papers.abstract: Pulsed field ablation (PFA) has emerged as a transformative approach for treating cardiac arrhythmias by exploiting irreversible electroporation to preferentially injure myocardium while limiting collateral damage. Translating this biophysical principle into safe and effective clinical systems requires careful integration of waveform design, catheter engineering, computational and experimental modelling, safety testing, and procedural workflow. This review summarizes the fundamental physical and engineering principles that govern cardiac PFA and examines how these principles influence efficacy, safety, lesion formation, and clinical usability. Electroporation is governed primarily by the local electric field and waveform-dependent lethal thresholds rather than generator voltage alone. Key waveform variables include monophasic vs. biphasic pulses, microsecond vs. nanosecond pulse widths, duty cycle, and total application duration. Catheter design further determines electric field distribution, lesion geometry, current density, and applicability across anatomic targets, with important distinctions between bipolar and monopolar configurations. Experimental and computational approaches used to investigate PFA include finite element simulations, cell culture systems, vegetal substrates, and in vivo animal models, each with distinct strengths and limitations. High-voltage pulse delivery can also produce unintended effects, including Joule heating, electrochemical reactions, bubble formation, arcing, and interactions with implanted electronic devices. These phenomena highlight the importance of optimized waveform design, electrode configuration, and safety monitoring. Clinical adoption depends not only on biological efficacy and safety but also on workflow efficiency, catheter versatility, procedure duration, mapping integration, anaesthesia requirements, and adaptability to differing clinical practices and geographic settings. The performance of a PFA system reflects the interaction of biophysics, waveform characteristics, catheter design, modelling, safety controls, and procedural usability. Understanding these interconnected principles is essential for developing PFA technologies that are effective, safe, predictable, and practical for contemporary electrophysiology laboratories.

papers.title: The future of PFA in cardiac ablation procedures.
papers.abstract: Pulsed field ablation (PFA) has rapidly emerged as a major development in catheter ablation, with increasing clinical adoption driven by procedural efficiency and a favorable safety profile compared with thermal energies. This article summarizes the future directions of PFA in electrophysiology, focusing on technological innovation, and how these advances are expected to expand PFA clinical indications. Additionally, this article provides a perspective on current gaps and future challenges of PFA. A perspective on future developments in new waveforms, catheter architectures, and integration with electroanatomical mapping systems for PFA is summarized. The document discusses novel waveform configurations and catheter design concepts that may improve lesion quality, procedural versatility, and safety. Additionally, this article also reviews how parallel advances in electroanatomical mapping integration, artificial intelligence, and robotic navigation are expected to enhance procedural guidance and enable individualized therapy. This manuscript summarizes the potential applications of PFA beyond pulmonary vein isolation and how emerging evidence supports its feasibility for linear atrial lesions, substrate modification, treatment of complex atrial tachycardias, and ventricular arrhythmia ablation. In addition, this article provides insights on how PFA may facilitate catheter ablation in new patient populations including elderly patients and those with higher procedural risks. Finally, this manuscript provides an outlook at major remaining challenges and knowledge gaps for PFA. The lack of homogenous procedural endpoints definitions and lesion durability assessment are discussed. Furthermore, this article highlights the need for standardized terminology and reporting in an environment where the high heterogeneity between available commercial systems complicates comparison across technologies.

papers.title: Nighttime Symptom Burden in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: A Qualitative Study.
papers.abstract: Nighttime symptoms are clinically important but understudied in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). This study explored patients' perceptions of nighttime symptoms, their effects on daily life, and symptom-management strategies. Thirty U.S. adults with COPD and moderate-to-high symptom burden (COPD Assessment Test score ≥10), without hospitalization or emergency department visits for severe exacerbation during the previous year, participated in semi-structured interviews. All participants received single-inhaler dual or triple maintenance therapy and completed the 7-item COPD and Asthma Sleep Impact Scal. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and thematically analyzed using the Symptom Management Theory framework. Participants (median age 63; 60% female; 90% White) reported a high burden of nighttime symptoms and sleep disruption (87% severely impacted based on CASIS). Participants described a pronounced nighttime symptom experience, most frequently shortness of breath, mucus/phlegm production, coughing, and difficulty staying asleep or frequent awakenings. A range of symptom management strategies was reported, including behavioral adaptations (routines, avoidance of technology, sleep hygiene), pharmacological management (antidepressants, sleep medications, rescue inhalers), and complementary and integrative approaches (meditation, acupuncture, relaxation techniques). Nighttime symptom outcomes extended beyond sleep disruption. Participants reported significant daytime consequences, including fatigue and impaired concentration. These effects contributed to activity avoidance and limitations in social participation. Among symptomatic patients receiving single-inhaler dual or triple maintenance therapy, nighttime COPD symptoms were commonly reported and were associated with substantial physical, emotional, and functional impacts. The findings support further consideration of nighttime symptoms in clinical assessment and individualized COPD management.

papers.title: Impaired Dynamic Cerebral Autoregulation Across the REM Sleep Behavior Disorder Spectrum: Evidence From Isolated REM Sleep Without Atonia to Parkinson's Disease With RBD.
papers.abstract: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is a parasomnia characterized by REM sleep without atonia (RSWA) and dream-enactment behaviors and is recognized as a prodromal manifestation of α-synucleinopathies. Isolated RSWA (iRSWA) has been proposed as a potential early stage within the RBD spectrum, although its clinical and physiological significance remains incompletely understood. This study aimed to investigate alterations in sleep architecture, phasic muscle activity, and dynamic cerebral autoregulation (dCA) across the spectrum from iRSWA to isolated RBD (iRBD) and Parkinson's disease with RBD (PD + RBD). We conducted a case-control study involving patients with iRSWA, iRBD, and PD + RBD, as well as age- and sex-matched healthy controls, based on video-polysomnography and magnetic resonance imaging. Scales for Outcomes in Parkinson's Disease-Autonomic Dysfunction (SCOPA-AUT) were used to evaluate the autonomic function. Transcranial Doppler and finger plethysmography were used to assess dCA by analyzing the phase difference using transfer function analysis. A total of 25 patients with iRSWA, 30 with iRBD, 28 with PD + RBD, and 30 healthy controls were included. REM sleep percentage was significantly lower in the iRBD and PD + RBD groups than in controls. Phasic RSWA, but not tonic RSWA, differed significantly among the three patient groups (p < 0.001). Phase difference was significantly lower in all three patient groups than in controls (p < 0.001) and was significantly associated with REM sleep amount and phasic RSWA (both p < 0.001). These findings suggest that dCA is impaired in patients with iRSWA, iRBD, and PD + RBD. Reduced phase difference was associated with lower REM sleep amount and greater phasic RSWA, suggesting disrupted coupling among REM sleep regulation, autonomic function, and cerebrovascular control. dCA dysfunction may represent an early pathophysiological feature in RBD-related neurodegeneration.
