papers.title: Coordinated mosquito biting dynamics at the human skin interface.
papers.abstract: The bite of a female mosquito is the critical point of pathogen transmission, yet the fine-scale biting dynamics on human skin remain unknown. Here, we combine high-speed videography, deep-learning-based tracking, and electrophysiology to analyze biting dynamics of the malaria vector Anopheles coluzzii in real time at the human skin interface. We uncover a previously uncharacterized synchronization of mouthpart and leg movements during probing and identify five distinct below skin sub-behaviors: piercing, vessel searching, blood ingestion, retraction, and withdrawal. We show that disruption of the orco and IR76b chemosensory genes can alter some components of normal biting but these effects are subtle, suggesting possible plasticity in direct-contact chemosensation and mosquito bite execution. Comparative analyses show genus-specific biting strategies between An. coluzzii and Aedes aegypti linked to distinct ways they find blood vessels. Our findings indicate that female mosquitoes exhibit a complex synchronization of body parts at the bite site via motor and chemosensory processes.

papers.title: The oral-sleep interface: Associations between oral health status and sleep outcomes in Canadian adults.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances and oral health problems are both prevalent public health concerns with substantial impacts on quality of life and systemic health. However, population-based evidence examining the independent associations between multiple dimensions of oral health and multiple sleep outcomes remains limited. This study investigated the associations between oral health indicators and sleep disturbances among Canadian adults using nationally representative survey data. We utilized data from adults aged 18 years and older who completed the 2017-2018 Canadian Community Health Survey (CCHS). Four oral health indicators were assessed: self-reported oral health, oral pain, bleeding gums, and dry mouth. Four sleep outcomes were examined: short sleep duration, insomnia symptoms, unrefreshing sleep, and difficulty staying awake. Multivariable logistic regression models were used, with progressive adjustment for sociodemographic factors, health status, and health behaviors. All four oral health indicators were significantly associated with most sleep outcomes in the full adjusted model. For short sleep duration, the strongest association was observed for poor oral health (AOR: 1.623). For insomnia symptoms, dry mouth (AOR: 1.904) and oral pain (AOR: 1.826) exhibited the strongest associations. For unrefreshing sleep, oral pain (AOR: 1.937) and dry mouth (AOR: 1.808) were associated with higher odds of reporting unrefreshing sleep. For difficulty staying awake, dry mouth (AOR: 1.720) and oral pain (AOR: 1.701) showed the strongest associations. Oral health problems are associated with multiple dimensions of sleep disturbance. These findings highlight the need for integrated care and complementary screening between dental and sleep medicine.

papers.title: Developing a systems-based programme theory for reducing night-time interactive electronic device use and improving sleep among adolescents.
papers.abstract: Adolescent night-time use of interactive electronic devices (IEDs) is increasingly linked to poor sleep, mental health challenges, and reduced academic performance. However, existing interventions often overlook the complex systems shaping these behaviours. This study presents a first-of-its-kind systems-based programme theory for CLOCK OFF - a peer influence intervention aimed at reducing night-time IED use and improving adolescent sleep - created through novel participatory mapping activities and analyses, which involved adolescents, parents and teachers. We conducted five online participatory workshops with adolescents (aged 11-14 years), parents, and teachers across four United Kingdom schools, supported by desk-based research. Workshop activities were facilitated using StickyStudio software. Causal loop diagramming was used to identify system components and feedback loops influencing adolescent IED use and sleep. Causal loop diagrams (CLDs) were iteratively built using Kumu software, refined and validated through stakeholder input and network analysis. The final CLD informed the development of a systems-based programme theory. Thirty participants (23 adolescents, 7 adults) contributed to the systems mapping process. The final CLD comprised 68 factors (i.e., causal influences of night-time IED use) and 131 connections between these factors, spanning behavioural, educational, psychological, physiological, social, and technological domains. CLOCK OFF-related mechanisms were represented across a large proportion of the system's identified feedback structures. The programme theory diagram included 72 factors and 147 feedback loops, grouped into five subsystems. These subsystems highlighted the dynamic interplay between enjoyment, overstimulation, fear of missing out (FOMO), emotional regulation, and educational stress. Participatory systems mapping with adolescents is a feasible and valuable method for surfacing complex behavioural drivers and informing intervention design. CLOCK OFF's systems-based programme theory offers a novel approach for understanding and addressing adolescent night-time IED use and sleep disruption. Findings support the need for multi-actor and peer-led, multi-level interventions embedded within broader systemic strategies.

papers.title: 24-hour movement behaviour composition associated with desired social-emotional functioning in the early years.
papers.abstract: Movement behaviours (sleep, sedentary behaviour, and physical activity) influence numerous health outcomes in children, including their social-emotional development. The optimal 24-hour movement behaviour composition for positive social-emotional development is unknown. The purpose of this study was to determine the movement behaviour composition across the 24-hour day associated with desired social-emotional functioning in the early years. This cross-sectional analysis included 560 children aged 1.2-2.9 years and 1,500 children aged 3.0-4.9 years from the Sleep and Activity Database (SADEY) for the Early Years study. Sedentary behaviour (SED), light physical activity (LPA), and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) were measured using ActiGraph accelerometers. Sleep duration was assessed using parent reports. Children social-emotional functioning was measured using the five domains of the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ), a widely used screening instrument of children's behaviours, emotions, and relationships across five domains (emotional problems, conduct problems, hyperactivity, peer problems, and prosocial behaviour). Compositional data analyses were used to estimate the 24-hour movement behaviour compositions associated with optimal scores for each of the SDQ domain z-scores and all five domains combined (the Goldilocks day). The movement behaviour composition was significantly associated with all five SDQ domains (all p < .01). For 1-2-year-olds, the Goldilocks day consisted of 12 h 12 min of sleep, 4 h 36 min of SED, 5 h 48 min of LPA, and 1h 24 min of MVPA. For 3-4-year-olds, it consisted of 12 h 08 min of sleep, 4 h 27 min of SED, 5 h 49 min of LPA, and 1 h 36 min of MVPA. The duration of total physical activity and MVPA associated with more favourable social-emotional functioning exceeded the minimum levels specified in the current 24-hour Movement Guidelines. These findings should not be interpreted as behavioural recommendations but rather as movement behaviour patterns associated with more favourable outcomes within this study population.

papers.title: Obesity in Children Aged 2 to 12 Years: A Review.
papers.abstract: Obesity affects 15% of children aged 2 to 5 years and 22% of children aged 6 to 11 years in the US. Obesity in children is associated with dyslipidemia, hypertension, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, and obstructive sleep apnea. Compared with normal-weight peers, children with obesity have lower quality of life and are 5 times more likely to have obesity in adulthood. Body mass index (BMI; calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) is used to identify children at risk for excess adiposity, and guidelines recommend that clinicians screen for obesity using BMI starting at age 2 years. Among children, obesity is defined using standardized age- and sex-specific growth charts, with obesity defined as BMI in the 95th or higher percentile and severe obesity as BMI of 120% or greater of the 95th percentile. Obesity treatment in children includes intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment, consisting of at least 26 contact hours of face-to-face group or family-based activities that incorporate nutrition, physical activity, and behavior change education delivered to the child and caregivers over a 3- to 12-month period. Intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment reduces BMI by 0.7 compared with children who do not participate in intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment. The only obesity pharmacotherapy currently approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for children younger than 12 years is setmelanotide, a melanocortin-4 receptor agonist, which is indicated for 3 forms of rare monogenic obesity (LEPR, POMC, and PCSK1 genetic variants), Bardet-Biedl syndrome, and acquired hypothalamic obesity. Liraglutide is currently only FDA approved for youth aged 12 years or older; however, a randomized clinical trial among children aged 6 to younger than 12 years demonstrated that, compared with placebo, liraglutide reduced BMI by 7.4%. Metabolic and bariatric surgery is rarely used in children younger than age 12 years and evidence supporting its use in children is limited. Early identification and treatment of obesity during childhood may reduce risk of type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and mortality in adulthood. Obesity in children is associated with chronic disease, such as hypertension, and with poor quality of life. Evidence-based treatment for obesity in children includes intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment, and pharmacotherapy may provide additional benefit, although short- and long-term safety and efficacy data are limited. Early identification and treatment of obesity during childhood may reduce risk of type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and mortality in adulthood.

papers.title: Association of childhood mild traumatic brain injury with mental and behavioral health outcomes later in life among U.S. Veterans: A LIMBIC-CENC study.
papers.abstract: Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) is a common injury across all age groups and populations, with a high prevalence among military service members and Veterans. The purpose of this cross-sectional study was to use a large, prospective cohort of Veterans to examine the association between childhood mTBI and multimodal mental and behavioral health outcomes, and among those with childhood mTBI, evaluate sociodemographic characteristics associated with worse outcomes. Data came from the Long-term Impact of Military-relevant Brain Injury Consortium-Chronic Effects of Neurotrauma Consortium (LIMBIC-CENC) prospective longitudinal study. This cohort included 1,286 Veterans, 61.3% of whom sustained a childhood mTBI. After adjustment for demographic, behavioral, and military history factors, Veterans with childhood mTBI had higher PTSD symptom scores (Mean Ratio[MR] = 1.36, 95%CI: 1.22-1.51), higher anger scores (MR = 1.08, 95%CI: 1.05-1.10), higher depression scores (MR = 1.31, 95% CI: 1.17-1.46), higher anxiety scores (mean difference [MD]= 4.3, 95% CI: 2.9-5.6), emotional-behavioral dyscontrol scores (MD = 3.2, 95% CI: 2.2-4.3), worse sleep quality (MD = 1.6, 95% CI: 1.1-2.2), worse neurobehavioral symptoms (MD = 6.8, 95% CI: 5.2-8.5), lower satisfaction with life (MD = -1.2, 95% CI: -2.1 to -0.27), and lower resilience scores (MR = 0.96, 95% CI: 0.94-0.99). There were no significant differences after adjustment for alcohol or drug use scores. Among individuals with a history of childhood mTBI, several mental and behavioral health outcomes were worse among those who sustained multiple mTBIs and better among those who were physically active and had higher education. These findings suggest markers of increased riskpresent before military enlistment that may warrant targeted prevention, screening, and treatment strategies. Increased awareness among healthcare providers may help identify Veterans with childhood mTBI history who would benefit from evidence-based treatment and support.

papers.title: Investigating the role of mental health and lifestyle behaviours in the risk of adolescent suicidal behaviours through machine learning.
papers.abstract: Suicidal behaviors among adolescents are a serious global public health concern and are closely linked to both mental health and everyday lifestyle behaviors. Suicidal ideation, planning, and attempts lie along a spectrum of increasing severity. However, how psychological distress and health-related behaviors interact to influence suicide risk is complex and not yet fully understood. This study aimed to identify key mental health and lifestyle factors associated with different stages of adolescent suicidal behaviors using interpretable machine learning methods. Data were obtained from the 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System (YRBS), a nationally representative survey of U.S. high school students. After data cleaning and multiple imputation, 16,946 adolescents aged 14-18 years were included in the analysis. Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) models were developed to predict suicidal ideation, suicide planning, and suicide attempts. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and related metrics. Feature importance was examined using gain-based measures, while SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and partial dependence plots were used to explore the direction, strength, and nonlinear effects of key predictors. All three XGBoost models showed satisfactory predictive performance. Mental health factors, particularly persistent feelings of sadness and self-rated mental health, were the strongest predictors across all stages of suicidal behaviors. Lifestyle behaviors, including sleep duration, physical activity, diet, screen time, and substance use, also contributed meaningfully to risk prediction, although their relative importance differed by outcome. SHAP analyses indicated that greater sadness and poorer mental health were strongly associated with higher suicide risk, whereas adequate sleep and higher levels of physical activity were associated with lower predicted risk. Substance use, including alcohol, cigarette, and marijuana use, played an important role in predicting suicide attempts than suicidal ideation or planning. Partial dependence analyses showed nonlinear and threshold effects, especially for sadness, mental health status, and sleep duration. Mental health factors, especially persistent sadness and overall psychological well-being, were among the most prominent factors associated with suicidal behaviors among adolescents, while lifestyle behaviors showed important and stage-specific associations. Interpretable machine learning approaches help identify complex and nonlinear patterns associated with adolescent suicide risk and offer valuable insights to guide targeted, evidence-based prevention efforts.

papers.title: Predicting mental health risk in adolescents using interpretable machine learning: Evidence from SHAP analysis.
papers.abstract: Adolescent mental health is a critical public health concern; however, the combined contribution of emotional, demographic, and behavioral factors to poor mental health remains incompletely understood. This study applied an interpretable machine learning framework to identify key predictors of elevated mental health risk among adolescents and characterize their relative and non-linear contributions. Data were drawn from the 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS), comprising 16,946 U.S. high school students. Elevated mental health risk was defined using the YRBS current mental health item (Q85): reporting that mental health was not good most of the time or always during the past 30 days. The distinct 12-month sadness/hopelessness item (Q25) was retained as a predictor in the primary XGBoost model. The operating threshold was selected by maximizing the Youden index using five-fold out-of-fold predictions in the training set and was then locked before evaluation in the held-out test set. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were used to assess feature importance and directional and non-linear patterns. Overall, 28.0% of adolescents were classified as having elevated mental health risk, with higher prevalence among females (39.9% vs. 16.9%) and peak prevalence at ages 16-17. The primary XGBoost model achieved an AUC of 0.806 and PR-AUC of 0.603. At the training-derived threshold of 0.285, accuracy was 0.749, sensitivity 0.754, specificity 0.747, and balanced accuracy 0.750. SHAP analysis identified sadness/hopelessness as the dominant predictor, followed by sex, sleep duration, screen time, and breakfast frequency. In a sensitivity analysis excluding sadness/hopelessness, discrimination decreased (AUC 0.736; PR-AUC 0.510). The revised primary model achieved balanced sensitivity and specificity above 0.700 using a threshold selected entirely within the training data. Sadness/hopelessness was the strongest predictor, while demographic and behavioral factors provided additional predictive information. Because sadness/hopelessness is conceptually close to the current mental health outcome and the data are cross-sectional, the model should be interpreted as an auxiliary risk-stratification tool rather than a standalone clinical screening or diagnostic instrument.

papers.title: EEG Edge-Centric Dynamics Reveal Distinct Post-Stroke Somatosensory Network Responses to Vibratory and Electrical Stimulation.
papers.abstract: Stroke-induced somatosensory deficits disrupt sensorimotor integration (SMI) and limit motor recovery, yet the immediate network-level effects of different somatosensory interventions remain unclear, hindering patient-specific rehabilitation planning. We propose an informatics framework based on edge-centric dynamic connectivity (ECDC) to characterize transient, whole-brain EEG network responses to sensory-level focal vibratory stimulation (FVS) and neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES). We analyzed EEG recordings from 15 chronic stroke participants and 15 healthy controls during forearm stimulation and quantified temporal network dynamics, spectral network organization, and interhemispheric interactions from instantaneous overlapping functional networks. Compared with NMES, FVS in stroke participants induced a distinct neurophysiological profile, including (i) shorter global theta-network latency, suggesting faster attentional engagement; (ii) higher contralesional alpha network diversity, indicating enhanced somatosensory recruitment; and (iii) reduced theta-alpha phase-amplitude coupling, reflecting decoupled interhemispheric interactions that may support adaptive reorganization. These findings provide interpretable network signatures for differentiating stimulation-specific brain responses and suggest a data driven route toward personalized SMI rehabilitation.
papers.journal: IEEE journal of biomedical and health informatics

papers.title: Strong mnemonic prediction errors increase cognitive control, attention, and arousal.
papers.abstract: Ongoing experience is continuously processed in the context of past events. Divergence between current experience and memory-based predictions (i.e., a mnemonic prediction error; MPE) is theorized to be a signal that encoding, as opposed to retrieval, should be prioritized. We asked how MPEs place demands on control and attention-related processes, and whether these demands differ as a function of prediction strength. We investigated these questions across two experiments, wherein we recorded scalp electroencephalography and/or pupillometry as 101 young human adults performed an associative memory task. Strong MPEs, more so than weak MPEs, increased physiological indices of cognitive control (frontal theta), attention (posterior alpha and pupil size), and arousal (pupil size). Greater cognitive control (frontal theta) during strong MPEs promoted better learning of prediction-violating (i.e., unexpected) stimuli. Collectively, these findings reveal multiple pathways through which the mind and brain respond adaptively to violations of strong mnemonic predictions.

papers.title: The effects of perinatal depression and anxiety on memory, attention, and cognitive flexibility: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Women in the perinatal period often report experiencing cognitive difficulties, such as forgetfulness, disorientation, and a reduced attention span. However, evidence from objective neuropsychological studies is inconsistent. Depressive and anxiety symptoms have been proposed as potential contributors to these cognitive challenges, with some studies suggesting a negative association between mood disturbances and cognitive performance during pregnancy and postpartum. This review aims to characterize the relationship between perinatal depressive and anxiety symptoms and cognitive functioning (memory, attention, and cognitive flexibility). Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science and PsycINFO electronic databases. Where at least three studies with comparable designs and outcomes were available, exploratory meta-analyses were conducted and are reported in supplementary material. We included 42 studies in the present review. The most consistent finding was a significant positive association between depressive symptoms and self-reported cognitive complaints across six studies. Results for objective tasks were inconsistent for working memory (k = 11), attention (k = 24), and cognitive flexibility (k = 5). Autobiographical memory was associated with depressive symptoms, but evidence was based on few studies (k = 3). Verbal memory (k = 8) and recognition memory (k = 2) were not associated with depressive or anxiety symptoms. Across domains, most studies were cross-sectional, relied on self-report symptom measures, used heterogeneous non-ecological cognitive tasks and rarely assessed anxiety, limiting the strength and generalizability of conclusions. Depressive symptoms are consistently associated with subjective cognitive complaints, but evidence for objective cognitive impairment in the perinatal period is inconclusive. The discrepancy between perceived and measured performance highlights the possible influence of mood, sleep, mental load, and sociocultural narratives on maternal cognition. More robust longitudinal and ecologically valid studies are needed to clarify these relationships and mechanisms, and to inform the development of targeted interventions.

papers.title: Sleep duration and prostate cancer-specific mortality in the Southern Community Cohort Study.
papers.abstract: Sleep patterns may affect metabolic and behavioral processes, which subsequently could be linked to cancer mortality. However, the relationship between sleep patterns and prostate cancer-specific mortality remains unclear. We evaluated the association of sleep and prostate cancer-specific mortality and investigated whether race/ethnicity influences the association. The Southern Community Cohort Study (SCCS), a prospective cohort study, recruited participants from 12 Southeastern states between March 2002 and September 2009. The cohort included 34,166 males, predominantly Black/African American. Sleep exposures were measured via a baseline questionnaire. Cox Proportional hazards models were used to estimate associations between sleep and prostate cancer-specific mortality and were adjusted for important potential confounders. During follow-up (median 15.9 years), 225 men died from prostate cancer. Longer sleep duration (≥ 9 hours) on weekends versus 7-8 hours was suggestively associated with an increased risk of prostate cancer-specific mortality (hazard ratio (HR)= 1.44, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.02-2.03). When stratified by race, longer sleep duration was suggestively associated with an increased risk of prostate cancer mortality for both Black and White men, although the associations were insignificant. Overall sleep duration and restless sleep were not associated with prostate cancer-specific mortality. Men reporting ≥ 9 hours of weekend sleep had an elevated risk of prostate cancer-specific mortality compared with those sleeping 7-8 hours. Stratified analysis suggests an increased risk of prostate cancer-specific mortality among both Black men and White men with ≥ 9 hours of sleep versus 7-8 hours, though estimates were imprecise due to small event numbers.

papers.title: Managing the transition without hormones.
papers.abstract: Perimenopause is a heterogeneous clinical transition characterized by fluctuating function of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis and a broad range of symptoms that frequently occur in overlapping clusters. Although menopause hormone therapy (MHT) is effective, many women require or prefer non-hormonal approaches, and several clinically relevant symptoms are not adequately addressed by MHT alone. This review summarizes evidence-based non-hormonal strategies for the management of vasomotor symptoms, sleep disturbance and fatigue, psychological and cognitive concerns, musculoskeletal complaints, and sexual, vulvovaginal and urinary issues. The article also proposes a structured, symptom-oriented clinical framework based on assessment of symptom burden and consideration for functional impact, patient priorities, comorbidities, contraindications and differential diagnoses. Management options include cognitive behavioral therapy, neurokinin receptor antagonists, selected antidepressants and other targeted pharmacotherapies, pelvic floor therapy and individualized lifestyle interventions. Treatment should be selected through shared decision-making, reassessed after a defined interval, and combined or escalated when response is insufficient. A structured algorithm can support consistent clinical decision-making while preserving the individualized and multidimensional care required during the menopausal transition.
papers.journal: Climacteric : the journal of the International Menopause Society

papers.title: Detecting Intraocular Pressure Harmonic Frequencies in Glaucoma and the Sampling Targets Needed to Identify Them With Self-Tonometry.
papers.abstract: The purpose of this study was to determine the detectability and occurrence of circadian and ultradian rhythms in patient-acquired intraocular pressure (IOP) measurements with sampling targets for reliable harmonic detection. A multi-harmonic non-uniform discrete Fourier transform (NDFT), with bootstrap amplitude confidence intervals and independent Lomb-Scargle periodogram (LSP) confirmation, was applied to 286 home-tonometry monitoring blocks from 137 eyes of 69 patients with glaucoma. Integer harmonic frequencies (F) from 1 to 10 cycles per day were tested. Characterized frequency was defined when noise-threshold significance, amplitude lower 95% confidence bound >0, and phase 95% confidence interval met prespecified criteria. Detection probability was modeled by a logistic generalized additive model (GAM) accounting for total observation count, clock-hour coverage, and the longest sparse-data gap. The 24-hour rhythm (F1) was characterized in 35.7% of blocks; at least one of F1, F2, F3, or F4 was characterized in 44.8% (128/286). Of these 128 blocks, 34% (43) had 2 or more harmonics simultaneously characterized and 7% (9) had 3 or more. Detected periodicities were almost exclusively integer harmonics. Non-integer LSP peaks arose in only 3.1% of blocks (9/286). Where 15 or more clock-hours contained at least 2 observations and no more than 2 consecutive clock-hours contained one or none, approximately 100 to 130 observations over 4 weeks gave a model-predicted detection probability of 75% to 85%, rising to 90% at approximately 150 observations. One or more characterizable 24-hour integer IOP harmonic rhythms could be detected with an appropriate self-tonometry protocol in nearly half of treated patients with glaucoma.

papers.title: Retatrutide Once Weekly for Treatment of Obstructive Sleep Apnea.
papers.abstract: Retatrutide, an investigational triple agonist of glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon-like peptide 1, and glucagon receptors, may be useful for treating obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). In two phase 3, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials nested within larger basket trials of once-weekly subcutaneous retatrutide, we assigned adults with moderate-to-severe OSA and a body-mass index (the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters) of at least 27, without (TRIUMPH-1-OSA) or with (TRIUMPH-2-OSA) type 2 diabetes, to receive retatrutide (4, 9, or 12 mg) or placebo. The primary end point was the change in the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI, the average number of apneas and hypopneas per hour of sleep) at 80 weeks with 9 mg and 12 mg of retatrutide. For OSA-related end points, a hybrid-treatment estimand was applied, with a hypothetical strategy used for participants who had intercurrent events suggesting treatment failure and a treatment-policy strategy used elsewhere. We also report intention-to-treat (ITT) results. A total of 243 participants underwent randomization in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and 448 in TRIUMPH-2-OSA. The baseline mean AHI was 58.6 and 55.9 events per hour, respectively, and the mean body weight was 119.6 and 115.9 kg. At 80 weeks, the mean changes in the AHI (hybrid-treatment estimand) with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-1-OSA were -22.9 (4 mg), -34.3 (9 mg), and -31.7 (12 mg) events per hour, versus -9.9 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -13.0 [95% confidence interval {CI}, -23.0 to -3.0], -24.4 [95% CI, -34.1 to -14.7], and -21.9 [95% CI, -32.2 to -11.5], respectively). The changes with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-2-OSA were -19.2 (4 mg), -24.7 (9 mg), and -25.4 (12 mg) events per hour, versus -10.3 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -8.9 [95% CI, -15.9 to -2.0], -14.4 [95% CI, -21.6 to -7.2], and -15.1 [95% CI, -22.5 to -7.7]). For the ITT estimand, the corresponding differences from placebo were -13.2 (95% CI, -22.6 to -3.9), -24.7 (95% CI, -34.1 to -15.3), and -22.5 (95% CI, -31.9 to -13.1) in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and -8.8 (95% CI, -15.8 to -1.7), -13.9 (95% CI, -21.3 to -6.6), and -15.0 (95% CI, -22.5 to -7.4) in TRIUMPH-2-OSA. The mean percent change in body weight with retatrutide (key secondary end point) was -12.5 to -22.2% in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and -12.1 to -18.5% in TRIUMPH-2-OSA, versus -4.8% and -5.6% with placebo (treatment-regimen estimand). The most common adverse events were gastrointestinal. In adults with OSA and obesity or overweight with or without type 2 diabetes, retatrutide resulted in significantly greater decreases in the AHI than placebo. (Funded by Eli Lilly; TRIUMPH-1 and -2 ClinicalTrials.gov numbers, NCT05929066 and NCT05929079.).
papers.journal: The New England journal of medicine

papers.title: Research Progress on the Precise Classification and Individualized Diagnosis and Treatment of Nocturia.
papers.abstract: Nocturia is a common urological symptom whose prevalence increases progressively with age. It not only impairs sleep and quality of life but also increases the risk of adverse events, including falls and fractures. Clinical management remains limited by inadequate evaluation of underlying etiologies, imprecise phenotyping, and suboptimal therapeutic responses. To facilitate standardized diagnostic and therapeutic strategies, we reviewed and summarized relevant literature published over the past decade. Focusing on four major subtypes, nocturnal polyuria (NP), diminished bladder capacity (DBC), global polyuria (GP), and sleep disorder-predominant nocturia (SDP), we developed a clinical framework integrating precise assessment, phenotypic classification, and individualized treatment. This review compares the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying different phenotypes, identifies the voiding diary as the cornerstone of assessment, and proposes a streamlined three-step clinical phenotyping algorithm. A stepwise treatment strategy tailored to different subtypes is outlined, incorporating psychological counseling, lifestyle modification, pharmacotherapy, physical therapy, and surgery. This review provides a reference for the precise and individualized management of nocturia and highlights the potential future roles of digital assessment and multidisciplinary care.

papers.title: The Sleep and Diet of Elite Female Australian Rules Football Athletes Differ With Age and Season Phase.
papers.abstract: The Australian Football League Women's (AFLW) competition is comprised of a short, intensive competitive season, highlighting the importance of proper fuelling and recovery to support performance. Little is known about the dietary and sleep habits of AFLW athletes across a season, and the influence that age has on these behaviours. Therefore, this study aimed to determine the effects of season phase and age on dietary intake and sleep in elite AFLW athletes. Dietary intake and sleep were assessed in 22 AFLW athletes (25.9 ± 5.0 y) over 10 nights, including five consecutive nights during both pre-season and in-season. Dietary intake was quantified through self-reported food diaries using a smartphone application (Easy Diet Diary), and sleep via a wearable monitoring device (Oura ring). Restricted maximum likelihood mixed models were used to determine variations in dietary intake and sleep in AFLW players between season phases (i.e., pre-season vs. in-season) and age. In-season protein (115.15 ± 35.14 vs. 126.48 ± 40.10 g, p = 0.026) and fat intakes (72.93 ± 29.55 vs. 83.43 ± 33.14 g, p = 0.012) were significantly lower compared to pre-season, with no differences in sleep measures observed between season phases. While age did not influence dietary intake, each additional year of age was associated with 8 min less sleep (p = 0.001) and 4 min earlier wake times (p = 0.032). These findings suggest that protein and fat intakes fluctuate across the seasons, with increasing age being a non-modifiable risk factor for shorter sleep durations within AFLW athletes.

papers.title: Adherence to the Age-Friendly Care 4Ms Framework and Association with Reduced Acute Care Utilization.
papers.abstract: The Age-Friendly Health Systems (AFHS) initiative emphasizes delivery of patient-centered, goal-concordant care for older adults through implementation of the Assess and Act-On care components of the 4Ms (What Matters Most, Medication, Mentation, and Mobility) framework. Despite broad adoption, there remains limited empirical evidence linking comprehensive, encounter-level adherence to 4Ms care with meaningful clinical and utilization outcomes. This retrospective study - designed through a multisite collaboration - evaluates the implementation of a standardized, informatics-driven approach to measure adherence to 4Ms care using electronic medical record (EMR) data and examines its association with hospital outcomes. The authors analyzed 40,411 inpatient encounters among adults 70 years of age or older admitted to acute care units across an eight-hospital health system between July 2024 and June 2025. Adherence to 11 operationalized 4Ms process measures was quantified at the encounter level based on expected care frequencies (shift, day, or visit based), incorporating both Assess (knowing the patient's 4Ms) and Act-On (incorporating the 4Ms into care delivery) components. A previously developed composite adherence score was used with tiered thresholds reflecting increasing fidelity of care delivery documentation. Primary outcomes included length of stay (LOS), discharge disposition, and 30-day unplanned readmissions. Multivariable regression models with inverse probability of treatment weighting were used to adjust for confounding. Overall documented adherence to 4Ms care varied considerably: On average, 75.3% of individual shift opportunities met compliance for aligning with age-friendly care guidance; however, 67% of encounters did not meet the initial threshold of adherence requiring 100% compliance with each opportunity to Assess throughout the encounter. Only 3% of encounters achieved higher-level documentation compliance (100% Assess and ≥50% Act-On). Although certain components, such as delirium screening and medication safety, demonstrated consistently high performance, substantial variability was observed in domains including mobility goal attainment, sleep optimization, and hydration. Higher documentation adherence to 4Ms care was strongly associated with shorter LOS, with the highest adherence tier demonstrating a 41% reduction in LOS (adjusted incident rate ratio, 0.59; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.57 to 0.60). In addition, higher adherence was associated with reduced odds of 30-day unplanned readmissions (adjusted odds ratio, 0.60; 95% CI, 0.45 to 0.79). The adjusted analyses revealed an association between higher documentation adherence and increased likelihood of discharge to postacute care facilities, most likely reflecting an interrelationship with patient complexity and functional status. These findings highlight the feasibility of a standardized, EMR-based measurement strategy for evaluating adherence to the 4Ms framework and underscore the importance of consistently documenting age-friendly care practices. Although 4Ms care was documented in only a minority of patients, reliable delivery across all care opportunities was associated with improved hospital efficiency and reduced acute care utilization, supporting its role as a scalable strategy for enhancing outcomes among hospitalized older adults. Further research is needed to define optimal pragmatic adherence definitions in relation to patient outcomes.
papers.journal: NEJM catalyst innovations in care delivery

papers.title: Acute creatine-guanidinoacetate supplementation improves regional brain oxygenation following sleep deprivation: A randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Background: Sleep deprivation impairs cognitive performance and may alter regional cerebral oxygenation. Nutritional strategies that preserve brain oxygenation could help mitigate these adverse effects. Aim: To compare the acute effects of creatine-guanidinoacetate (GAA), molecular hydrogen inhalation, caffeine, and placebo on regional brain oxygenation and attention-related performance following sleep deprivation.Methods: Twenty-two healthy young adults completed a 24-hour sleep deprivation protocol and were randomly assigned to receive creatine-GAA, molecular hydrogen inhalation, caffeine, or placebo. Brain oxygenation was assessed using functional near-infrared spectroscopy over the frontal, temporal, and occipital cortices during a modified attention network test. Alertness, executive control, orienting, reaction time, and accuracy were also evaluated.Summary: Creatine-GAA significantly increased frontal oxygen saturation (50.8% ± 4.1% to 61.0% ± 5.9%, P = 0.01; Cohen's d = 2.00) and temporal oxygen saturation (63.1% ± 4.8% to 70.2% ± 2.6%, P = 0.01; Cohen's d = 1.83). Significant time-by-treatment interactions were observed for frontal oxygen saturation (P = 0.043; ηp2 = 0.331), temporal oxygen saturation (P = 0.021; ηp2 = 0.428), and occipital total hemoglobin (P = 0.022; ηp2 = 0.405). No significant between-group differences were observed in attention-related outcomes. Acute creatine-GAA supplementation improved regional brain oxygenation following sleep deprivation, particularly in the frontal and temporal cortices, without measurable improvements in attention-related performance. These preliminary findings support further investigation of creatine-based nutritional strategies in larger randomized controlled trials.

papers.title: Actigraphy-based characterization of nighttime repositioning in individuals with spinal cord injury living in the community setting to facilitate pressure injury risk assessment.
papers.abstract: Observational cohort study. To introduce an actigraphy-based method for objectively measuring in-bed mobility during sleep in individuals with spinal cord injury (SCI) living in the community, and to assess the feasibility and safety of this approach, as well as its association with pressure injury (PI) incidence. Community-dwelling individuals with traumatic SCI. Nighttime repositioning habits were assessed in 28 individuals with traumatic SCI, of whom 20 were included in the final analysis. An actigraph placed on the sternum recorded in-bed repositioning frequency and time spent in different positions for up to 14 consecutive nights. Participants spent most of their sleep time in the supine (73%) or lateral (25%) position. In-bed repositioning occurred at an average of 2.2 ± 2.4 times per night, with large interindividual variability reflecting heterogeneous neurological levels and functional status. Only 10% of subjects repositioned at least once every 3 hours during the night. Within 1 year, 40% of individuals developed a PI, and these participants had repositioned significantly less frequently at night compared with those without PI (1 ± 1 vs. 3 ± 2 instances of repositioning per night, P = 0.01). Actigraphy provides a safe and objective method for assessing nocturnal repositioning behaviors in community-dwelling individuals with SCI. Reduced nighttime repositioning frequency was associated with a higher incidence of PI, supporting the clinical utility of objective mobility assessment for PI risk evaluation.
papers.journal: The journal of spinal cord medicine

papers.title: CIRP: New Horizons for CNS Injury Biomarkers and Therapy.
papers.abstract: Cold-inducible RNA-binding protein (CIRP) is a stress-response protein that protects cells under conditions of low temperature and other stresses. The expression of CIRP is induced by various stressors. CIRP regulates gene expression through complex, multi-layered mechanisms and plays a central role in physiological and pathological processes, including cell proliferation, apoptosis, inflammatory responses, and circadian rhythms. In central nervous system (CNS) injuries, CIRP exhibits a dual role. Intracellular CIRP has a neuroprotective function. In contrast, when released into the extracellular space as eCIRP, it acts as a damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) that exacerbates neuroinflammation. Serum levels of eCIRP are significantly elevated in patients with CNS injuries, such as acute ischemic stroke and intracerebral hemorrhage, suggesting its potential as a biomarker for diagnosis and prognosis. Furthermore, targeting the eCIRP signaling pathway has shown significant therapeutic effects in various models of neurological injury. Strategies include using inhibitory peptides like C23 and M3, as well as microRNA-based approaches. Here, we systematically review the molecular characteristics, expression regulation, and biological functions of CIRP, with a focus on its neuroprotective role, biomarker potential, and therapeutic targeting in CNS injuries.

papers.title: Indolizine-Based Small-Molecule Fluorescent Probes for Ex Vivo Imaging of Amyloid-β Plaques.
papers.abstract: Fluorescence probes for visualizing amyloid-β (Aβ) plaques are important tools in Alzheimer's disease (AD) research. We synthesized a library of 49 indolizine derivatives using a modular synthetic approach and evaluated their fluorescence labeling behavior directly in ex vivo brain tissue sections from 5XFAD transgenic mice. Through an ex vivo tissue-based screening workflow using anti-Aβ antibody 6E10 as a reference standard for plaque-containing regions, five hit compounds (YIZ-20, YIZ-32, YIZ-36, YIZ-45, and YIZ-47) displaying plaque-associated fluorescence patterns were identified. Costaining experiments demonstrated spatial correspondence between probe fluorescence and antibody-defined plaque regions. Spectral analysis showed that the selected YIZ probes exhibited emission profiles with somewhat reduced overlap with the Hoechst 33342 channel compared with thioflavin S (ThS), providing a modest but practical advantage for multichannel imaging applications. These findings highlight the utility of ex vivo tissue-based screening for fluorescent-probe discovery and establish indolizine as a promising scaffold for the development of complementary fluorescence imaging tools for AD-related ex vivo tissue studies.

papers.title: Serotonin Neurobiology and Artificial Intelligence-Driven Biomarker Detection in Affective Disorders: A Comprehensive Review.
papers.abstract: Affective disorders, including major depressive disorder (MDD) and generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), impose a major global health burden because of their high prevalence, early onset, disability, and substantial social and economic impacts. Diagnosis remains challenging because it relies largely on subjective clinical assessment and symptom-based criteria, which often delay recognition and contribute to heterogeneous treatment response. Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, 5-HT) has long been central to the understanding of these disorders, but the classical serotonin hypothesis has evolved into a broader systems-level framework in which serotonergic dysfunction is linked with neurotransmission, receptor signaling, transporter regulation, neuroplasticity, endocrine balance, immune modulation, circadian rhythm control, and gut-brain communication. Serotonin biosynthesis, metabolism, and compartmentalization are tightly regulated, and variation in the serotonin transporter and related pathways influences vulnerability to disease, symptom expression, and response to therapy. Although serotonin-targeted pharmacotherapy remains foundational, its delayed and variable clinical effects highlight the need for objective biomarkers and more-precise monitoring strategies. This Review gives a comprehensive overview of serotonin neurobiology in affective disorders and the therapeutic implications of serotonergic dysregulation. It discusses the current understanding of serotonin synthesis, receptor heterogeneity, transporter function, and broader system interactions that shape mood, stress responsivity, and treatment outcomes. The Review also examines the growing role of artificial intelligence in psychiatric biomarker discovery, including machine learning and deep learning approaches applied to neuroimaging, electrophysiology, physiological signals, and language-based data for improved diagnosis and prediction of antidepressant responses. In addition, emerging serotonin-specific biosensors are discussed as promising tools for real-time, noninvasive neurochemical monitoring. By integrating mechanistic insights into serotonin biology with AI-based analytics and biosensing technologies, this Review highlights a pathway toward more objective, personalized, and effective management of affective disorders.

papers.title: Associations Between Biomarkers of Alzheimer's Disease and Sleep in Cognitively Unimpaired Older Adults.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances have been implicated as a risk factor for developing Alzheimer's disease (AD), but evidence linking plasma AD biomarkers to sleep in cognitively unimpaired individuals remains limited. The present study examined associations between evening, morning, and overnight changes in plasma AD biomarkers and measures of sleep macro- and microstructure and subjective sleep quality in older adults. Forty cognitively unimpaired adults aged 55 to 75 years (20 females) without sleep or mental disorders underwent overnight polysomnography. Plasma AD biomarkers p-tau181, p-tau217, t-tau, Aβ42, Aβ40, and Aβ42/40 were assessed in the evening and in the morning and related to sleep macro- and microstructure (sleep spindles, EEG spectral power), and subjective sleep measures by using correlational analyzes. Higher evening t-tau and p-tau181 were associated with reduced N3 sleep, whereas higher morning t-tau and greater overnight increases in t-tau were related to longer nocturnal wakefulness. Amyloid-β measures showed the most consistent associations with sleep microstructure. Higher Aβ42 and Aβ40 concentrations were associated with shorter duration and lower density of sleep spindles, particularly at frontal sites. Higher evening and morning amyloid-β concentrations were also associated with lower alpha, beta, and spindle-frequency EEG power, mainly during non-rapid eye movement sleep. Tau associations with EEG spectral power were less consistent. In cognitively unimpaired older adults, plasma AD biomarkers were associated with PSG sleep features, especially amyloid-β markers with sleep microstructure. These exploratory, correlational findings suggest that sleep spindles and spectral power may reflect early AD-related biological processes but require replication in larger cohorts.
papers.journal: Annals of clinical and translational neurology

papers.title: Artificial intelligence applications in intracranial electroencephalography for epilepsy management: Insights from AI in Epilepsy 2025.
papers.abstract: Intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) provides direct recordings of cortical activity and remains central to the presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant focal epilepsy. However, the high dimensionality and complexity of iEEG data increasingly challenge conventional visual interpretation. Artificial intelligence (AI) methods have accelerated quantitative analyses in electrophysiology, supporting localization, outcome prediction, and therapeutic decision-making in epilepsy. This article reviews recent advances in the application of AI to iEEG in epilepsy and in particular stereo-EEG, although the concepts discussed are broadly relevant across iEEG modalities. Although many of these approaches have shown encouraging results, the current evidence remains largely preliminary, with most studies being retrospective, single-center investigations that lack independent external validation. AI-based integration of iEEG with multimodal magnetic resonance imaging shows promise for improving surgical planning in drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Concurrently, early studies suggest that AI-driven iEEG analysis may enhance epileptogenic zone identification by detecting subtle electrophysiological signatures, network interactions, and temporal dynamics. These multimodal frameworks emphasize distributed epileptic networks rather than isolated focal abnormalities. AI is also reshaping how iEEG-guided stimulation is designed and interpreted. Data-driven approaches have the potential to optimize stimulation parameters, predict network responses, and clarify mechanisms underlying diagnostic and therapeutic stimulation, laying the groundwork for adaptive, patient-specific neuromodulation. Beyond short-term epilepsy monitoring, AI applications increasingly incorporate continuous sensing, longitudinal network modeling, and integration with implantable neurotechnology platforms. Although these developments require prospective multicenter studies with external validation before widespread clinical implementation, advances in multimodal data integration, interpretable modeling, and continuous sensing position AI-enhanced iEEG as an emerging platform for precision brain network medicine for epilepsy.

papers.title: The influence of circadian variables on ecotoxicology metabolomics.
papers.abstract: Ecotoxicologists are using metabolomics increasingly to gain insight into toxicological mechanisms and sublethal effects of chemical exposures. Metabolomics offers a sensitive multi-parameter approach that can detect biochemical responses not obvious using apical and behavioural endpoints. This includes the responses to very low-dose toxicant exposures, variations in the physico-chemical state of experimental media, and even the progression of circadian rhythms. Consequently, repeatability and comparability of metabolomics experiments relies on the control and reporting of these features. In this systematic quantitative literature review, we examine recent ecotoxicology research to determine the rate and quality of reporting of circadian timing and other variables that influence circadian rhythms and the associated metabolome. We found that most circadian variables are underreported and call for further research into the influence of their manipulation on the metabolome.
papers.journal: Biological reviews of the Cambridge Philosophical Society

papers.title: Altitude-induced plasticity of respiratory central-peripheral chemoreflex interaction.
papers.abstract: Stable breathing depends on the integrated action of central and peripheral chemoreceptors, but the nature of this interaction in humans and its physiological importance remain controversial. Previous studies reported additive, hypo-additive and hyper-additive responses across species, preparations and protocols. Here, we used a novel method to quantify peripheral chemoreflex sensitivity across graded levels of central chemoreceptor activation to test whether central-peripheral chemoreceptor interaction in awake humans is fixed or state dependent. At low altitude, the form of interaction varied across individuals, with most showing additive responses (12/17) and a substantial subset showing hypo-additivity (5/17). After 7-10 days of acclimatization to 3500 m, all five hypo-additive individuals became additive, and four additive participants became hyper-additive. This shift in interaction towards hyper-additivity provides the first evidence that central-peripheral chemoreceptor integration is plastic. Plasticity during wakefulness was not associated with individual differences in central sleep apnoea severity at high altitude. Thus, our findings confirm that central-peripheral chemoreceptor interaction differs among individuals and suggest that the form of interaction can be reshaped by hypobaric hypoxic stress. KEY POINTS: How central and peripheral chemoreceptor drives to breathe interact in humans and whether this process is plastic remains uncertain. We quantified peripheral chemoreflex sensitivity to hypoxia (PChS) across graded levels of central chemoreceptor activation at low altitude and after 7-10 days of high-altitude exposure (3500 m). Seventeen participants performed repeated modified rebreathing tests with end-tidal P O 2 fixed at 150 (hyperoxia), 60 and 45 mmHg (hypoxia). PChS was computed at 1 mmHg intervals of end-tidal P C O 2 ( P ETC O 2 ) from linear regression of the difference in ventilation between hypoxic and hyperoxic conditions vs. calculated arterial oxygen saturation (ScO2) (L·min-1·mmHg-1·%ScO2 -1). At low altitude, PChS increased with P ETC O 2 in all individuals; the relationship was linear (no interaction) in 12 participants, and 5 showed hypo-additivity. After acclimatization, central and peripheral chemoreflex sensitivities increased. All hypo-additive individuals became additive; four additive individuals became hyper-additive. Central-peripheral chemoreceptor interaction is plastic in humans and can shift towards hyper-additivity with sustained hypobaric hypoxia.

papers.title: Patterns of Sleep Inequities by Experiences and Recognition of Multiple Types of Discrimination Among Members of Three Urban Community Health Centers: The Life + Health Study (2020-2022).
papers.abstract: Discrimination and unfair treatment are pervasive and contribute to population health inequities. This study examined how implicit and explicit measures of recognition of discrimination toward target vs. dominant groups, preference for target vs. dominant groups, and self-reported measures of experiences of discrimination are associated with sleep duration, disturbance, and impairment. Life + Health was a cross-sectional study that enrolled 699 participants ages 25-64 from three community health centers in Boston, MA between May 2020 and August 2022. We assessed implicit and explicit measures of six types of discrimination-racism, sexism, heterosexism, cissexism, ageism, and sizeism-and used regression-based modeling to assess crude and adjusted associations of measures with sleep outcomes. We found that target groups generally reported shorter sleep duration and worse sleep disturbance and impairment than dominant groups, though only shorter sleep duration among People of Color remained significant in adjusted models. Associations between implicit and explicit measures and sleep outcomes were largely attenuated after adjustment, though independent effects emerged for sexism among women in relation to sleep impairment. Findings highlight the complex relationships of recognition of discrimination and implicit preferences with sleep health and the importance of multidimensional approaches to measuring discrimination. Future longitudinal and larger sample population studies are needed to clarify mechanisms, consider intersectional identities and experiences, and identify intervention targets to advance sleep equity and population health. Our findings highlight the necessity of funding rigorous research on discrimination and health; defunding such research undermines scientific integrity, public health, and the goal of ensuring that all populations can thrive.

papers.title: Piezoelectric actuator-evoked mechano-gated currents in trigeminal neurons innervating the mouse temporomandibular joint.
papers.abstract: The most burdensome symptom of temporomandibular joint disorders (TMJDs) is mechanically evoked pain. To identify the trigeminal ganglion (TG) neuronal subtypes mediating mechanical sensitivity, we combined whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology with immunohistochemistry (IHC) to characterize mouse TMJ-innervating TG neurons retrogradely labeled from the TMJ. Electrophysiological analysis identified five distinct neuronal groups, only one of which responded to piezo actuator-induced mechanical stimulation. TMJ innervation was dominated by C- and A-nociceptors, comprising four of the five identified groups. The fifth, a minor population of small-diameter neurons (S1), displayed properties consistent with either vGlut3-positive, C-low-threshold mechanoreceptors (C-LTMRs) or Sst-positive neurons. Two mechanically insensitive C-nociceptor groups, distinguished by their action potential firing patterns, likely corresponded to CGRP-positive and non-Mrgpr neuronal populations. One mechanically insensitive A-nociceptor group likely represented Smr2-positive Aδ high-threshold mechanoreceptors (Aδ-HTMRs). The only mechanically responsive neurons were large-diameter A-nociceptors, which likely correspond to the weakly TrkC- expressing neuronal population. No recorded neurons displayed electrophysiological characteristics of classical A-LTMRs. Together, these findings demonstrate that the TMJ is innervated by a distinct repertoire of TG sensory neurons compared with the skin and masseter muscle, with mechanically responsive afferents restricted to a single A-nociceptor subtype rather than classical low-threshold mechanoreceptors.

papers.title: A First Case of Compulsive Amnestic Sleep-Related Shopping Induced by Pramipexole Therapy of Restless Legs Syndrome.
papers.abstract: Dopamine receptor agonists (DAs) such as pramipexole/ropinirole are recognized treatments for restless legs syndrome (RLS) and Parkinson's disease (PD). It is well established that these medications can cause impulse control disorders (ICDs) during wakefulness, side effects with serious and potentially life-altering consequences. Impulse control disorders are recurrent difficult-to-resist behaviors that can be harmful to the patient or others around them. Common examples include pathologic gambling and compulsive sexual behaviors, eating, and shopping. We present the case of a patient with RLS who developed pathologic nocturnal sleep-related shopping, without recalling the events, which resolved after discontinuing pramipexole. This case illustrates the devastating consequences that unrecognized medically-induced ICDs can have on patients' lives and the importance of counseling patients about ICDs during wake and sleep prior to starting DA therapy.

papers.title: Diaphragm 'atonia' during ictal and post-ictal apnoea: A case report.
papers.abstract: Ictal and post ictal central apnoea (ICA and PCA) are driven by suppression of brainstem respiratory drive and represent an electroclinical biomarker of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP). While animal models have demonstrated a true 'atonic diaphragm' underlying seizure-related apnoea, no human polygraphic study has yet confirmed respiratory muscle 'atonia' with direct EMG recording. In this case report, we present a 26-year-old female with meningoencephalocele-associated temporal lobe epilepsy who underwent a video-EEG polygraphy integrated with surface EMG from intercostals muscles and the diaphragm. We recorded a left frontotemporal seizure with ICA and four consecutives PCA events, all accompanied by surface electromyographic silence of the diaphragm and the intercostal muscles. This case provide a human polygraphic evidence of diaphragm and intercostal muscles silence during ICA and PCA, confirming the cascade of respiratory inhibition through brainstem respiratory centres down to respiratory muscles themselves. Notably, muscles relaxation occurred despite the patient was awake and able to follow commands. These findings support the importance of cardiorespiratory polygraphy during presurgical video-EEG evaluation, especially for temporal lobe seizures, to identify patients at higher SUDEP risk.

papers.title: Frontal Asymmetry in Infancy: Predictive Utility for Distinct Patterns of Temperament.
papers.abstract: Recent theorizing has emphasized motivational systems, rather than specific emotional reactions, when interpreting frontal asymmetry. We examined the predictive utility of infant electroencephalogram (EEG) frontal asymmetry during two approach-oriented tasks within 82 mother-infant dyads (infant age: M = 38.88 weeks, SD = 8.13 weeks; infant ethnicity: 86.7% Caucasian; infant sex: 51.2% female). Peek-a-Boo (PAB) and Toy Removal (TR) were chosen as predictors of mother-reported temperament, as both elicit approach motivation via a blocked goal in a joyful and frustrating context, respectively. TR asymmetry effect on Surgency/Positive Affectivity (SPA) was observed and driven primarily by a significant predictive relationship between TR asymmetry and Smiling and Laughter, f2 = 0.31. Negative Emotionality (NE) related outcomes were predicted by TR asymmetry, driven by Sadness, f2 = 0.20. Other than occasional contributions of covariates, no additional statistically significant results were noted. These findings are discussed as most consistent with the capability model of lateralization.

papers.title: Drosophila Appl loss disrupts proteins in mitochondrial oxidative and glycosylation pathways conserved in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: The physiological functions of the amyloid precursor protein (APP) remain unclear due to genetic redundancy and complex phenotypes. For decades, Drosophila amyloid precursor protein-like (Appl) research has relied on Appl d, a presumed null allele generated by irradiation. Here, we show that Appl d contains complex chromosomal rearrangements and background mutations confounding the interpretation of gene function. To address this, we created a precise CRISPR toolkit, including a clean null and a reporter allele. Deep proteomic profiling reveals that true Appl loss affects proteins associated with N-linked glycosylation, mitochondrial, and metabolic functions in a distinct signature from the background of Appl d. This conserved metabolic signature mirrors alterations in human patients and mouse Alzheimer's models and is associated with disrupted sleep and locomotion in flies. Our findings correct the genetic understanding of Appl, establishing it as a conserved regulator of metabolic balance essential for neuronal function.

papers.title: A 6-8-Hour Nighttime Sleep Strategy and Subsequent Cognitive Performance: A Target Trial Emulation Study.
papers.abstract: Sleep duration is a modifiable factor linked to cognitive aging among middle-aged and older adults, but existing evidence is largely correlational. Using observational data in which sleep duration was self-reported, we emulated a target trial to estimate the effect of maintaining a 6-8 h nighttime sleep strategy on subsequent cognitive performance. This target trial emulation study analyzed participants from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), a longitudinal, nationally representative prospective cohort of Chinese adults aged 45 years and older, and followed them from 2011 to 2020. Nocturnal sleep duration was self-reported at every wave. The 6-8 h sleep strategy was compared with a non-6-8 h strategy (<6h or >8h) using intention-to-treat (ITT), per-protocol (PP), and inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW)-weighted PP analyses. Primary outcome was the total cognitive score (range 0-21) after 9 years. Groups were balanced by 1:1 propensity-score matching (PSM) on 18 baseline covariates, and missing baseline covariate data were handled by multiple imputation by chained equations. Of 8147 eligible participants, 2341 matched pairs were included after PSM. The 6-8 h sleep strategy was consistently associated with higher cognitive scores than the non-6-8 h strategy in the ITT analysis (β = 0.237, 95% CI 0.016 to 0.458, p=0.036), the unweighted PP analysis (β = 0.394, 95% CI -0.013 to 0.801, p=0.058), and the IPCW-weighted PP analysis (β = 0.614, 95% CI 0.176 to 1.052, p=0.006). All estimates were modest in absolute terms, corresponding to 5.3% and 13.7% of one standard deviation of the outcome for the ITT and weighted PP analyses. The dose-response curve showed a nonlinear, inverted U-shaped association (P for non-linearity <0.001), with the highest predicted cognition at about 6.7 h of sleep. Neither sex nor age modified the association (P for interaction 0.84 and 0.27). By emulating a target trial with repeated prospective cohort data, this study moves beyond simple association and suggests that maintaining 6-8 h of self-reported nighttime sleep is associated with modestly higher subsequent cognitive performance. Target trial emulation improves the rigour of effect estimation but does not eliminate residual confounding, exposure misclassification or selective attrition; the findings require confirmation in studies using objective sleep assessment and more complete control of time-varying confounding.

papers.title: Impact of motor guided imagery therapy on stroke patients with pain symptoms: a three-level meta-analysis and systematic review of randomized controlled trials.
papers.abstract: Post-stroke pain is a common and intractable complication that hinders neurorehabilitation progress. Motor Guided Imagery (MGI), an emerging rehabilitation technique based on brain-computer interaction principles, has shown potential in relieving post-stroke pain, yet high-quality evidence on its multi-dimensional efficacy remains insufficient. This study aimed to systematically evaluate the effects of MGI on pain, sensorimotor function, sleep quality, life status, and psychological mood in stroke patients using a three-level meta-analysis. This study aimed to quantitatively assess the therapeutic effects of Motor Guided Imagery for stroke-related pain and explore potential intervention moderators using a three-level meta-analysis framework. Eight Chinese and English databases were searched from inception to June 29, 2025, to collect randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of MGI for stroke patients with pain. A three-level random-effects model was adopted to pool Hedges' g effect sizes, accompanied by heterogeneity testing, moderator analysis, influence analysis, and publication bias assessment. Influence-based outlier detection was implemented; analyses retaining all effect-size observations were treated as the primary main analysis, while outlier-removed analyses were reported only as supplementary sensitivity checks. Motor-guided imagery training significantly relieved pain (g = -0.524, 95% CI -0.779 to -0.269, p = 0.0006; negative Hedges' g indicates clinical improvement for this outcome) and improved sleep quality (g = -1.658, 95% CI -2.115 to -1.201, p < 0.001; negative Hedges' g indicates clinical improvement for this outcome) in stroke patients. Meanwhile, it significantly enhanced motor function (g = 1.395, 95% CI 0.963 to 1.826, p < 0.001), life status (g = 1.757, 95% CI 0.966 to 2.549, p = 0.0012), and psychological-emotional status (g = 1.729, 95% CI 1.045 to 2.413, p = 0.0002); positive Hedges' g indicates clinical improvement for the latter three outcomes. Moderator analysis indicated that acute-phase intervention (≤4 weeks) and high-frequency regimens (>5 sessions/week) tended to produce better analgesic effects, while age, gender, single-session duration, and pain location had no significant moderating effects. MGI may produce beneficial rehabilitation effects that can alleviate post-stroke pain and synergistically improve motor function, sleep, daily-living ability, and psychological state of stroke patients. Exploratory subgroup trends indicated potentially larger effects for early implementation within the acute phase and high-frequency short-duration regimens. However, these observations should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating clues given non-significant overall moderator tests. Further high-quality research is required to confirm these findings. The systematic review protocol was retrospectively registered with PROSPERO under registration ID CRD420261278812, after literature search and full-text screening had been completed. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261278812; identifier: CRD420261278812.

papers.title: Context-specific hypermetabolism in humans with mitochondrial defects.
papers.abstract: Pathogenic mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) defects test how impaired oxidative phosphorylation reshapes human energy expenditure. We studied adults with confirmed mtDNA defects (MitoD) and healthy controls using whole-room indirect calorimetry, doubly labeled water, quantitative magnetic resonance, actigraphy, autonomic monitoring, mood assessments, plasma inflammatory markers, and growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15). Under behaviorally clamped conditions, fat-free mass-adjusted 24-h energy expenditure (24-h EE) was consistently higher in MitoD, with higher non-resting expenditure per unit wrist acceleration by day, and blunted sleep-related metabolic suppression at night. In contrast, free-living total daily energy expenditure (TDEE) was similar between groups despite lower physical activity in MitoD, consistent with behavioral compensation within a constrained energy budget. Plasma GDF15 was ~5-fold higher in MitoD and tracked with disease severity, systemic inflammation, fatigue, energetic burden, and lower habitual activity. These findings identify a persistent energetic burden in MitoD that is buffered in daily life and associated with elevated GDF15.

papers.title: Relative Brain Perfusion Differences and Cognitive Improvement During Multimodal Management in a Patient With Progressive Cognitive Symptoms: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Progressive cognitive symptoms in older adults may reflect multiple interacting neurologic, vascular, sleep-related, medical, and lifestyle factors, making both etiologic attribution and assessment of treatment response challenging. We report the case of a 72-year-old man with approximately five years of progressive cognitive symptoms, including short-term memory impairment, slowed processing, distractibility, reduced initiative, and executive difficulties, in the setting of a remote cardiac arrest, cardiovascular and cerebrovascular risk, subsequent head trauma, and suspected sleep-disordered breathing. Baseline evaluation included a Self-Administered Gerocognitive Examination (SAGE) score of 9/22, minimal depressive symptoms, continuous performance testing, and adjunctive resting and concentration brain perfusion single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT). The SPECT findings were interpreted qualitatively as differences in relative regional tracer distribution and were not considered independently diagnostic. An individualized multimodal management plan emphasized sleep and circadian regularity, Mediterranean-style dietary measures, hydration, gradual aerobic and resistance exercise, cognitive and social engagement, and nonprescription nutritional supplementation without psychotropic medication. Over approximately six months, the patient and his wife reported improvement in memory, attention, organization, communication, motivation, and overall cognitive clarity, accompanied by renewed reading and cycling activity. Repeat SAGE increased by 9 points, from 9/22 to 18/22. Because several interventions were implemented concurrently, no single treatment component can be assigned a causal effect, and spontaneous improvement, natural variability, regression toward the mean, and practice effects cannot be excluded as contributors to the observed change. This case suggests that meaningful cognitive improvement may occur during individualized, multimodal longitudinal care while underscoring the importance of repeated reassessment and cautious interpretation of adjunctive brain perfusion SPECT.
